title: Chapter 10: Analysis of Categorical Data
text:
Key ideas

Categorical Data
Categorical data record which group, class, brand, color, outcome, or category each observation belongs to. Instead of analyzing means, we usually analyze counts or proportions in each category.


Multinomial Response Model
When each trial results in exactly one of \(k\) possible categories, the counts follow a multinomial model. If the category probabilities are \[
p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k,
\] then they must satisfy \[
p_1+p_2+\cdots+p_k=1.
\] The binomial model is the special case where \(k=2\).


Expected Counts
Under the null hypothesis, each category has a hypothesized probability. The expected count in category \(i\) is \[
E_i = np_i.
\] These expected counts describe what we would expect to see if the null hypothesis were true.


Chi-square Goodness-of-Fit Statistic
The goodness-of-fit test compares observed counts to expected counts: \[
\chi^2 =
\sum
\frac{(\text{observed count} - \text{expected count})^2}
{\text{expected count}}.
\] Large values of \(\chi^2\) mean the observed counts are far from what the null hypothesis predicts.


Degrees of Freedom and P-value
For a goodness-of-fit test with \(k\) categories, the test statistic is compared to a chi-square distribution with \[
k-1
\] degrees of freedom. The P-value is the area to the right of the observed test statistic.


Sample Size Assumption
The chi-square approximation works well when the expected counts are large enough. A common rule is that every expected cell count should be at least 5.

title: Chapter 9: Simple Linear Regression
text:
Key ideas

Simple Linear Regression Model
Simple linear regression models the relationship between one quantitative response variable \(Y\) and one quantitative predictor \(x\) using a straight line. The model is written as
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + \varepsilon_i.
\]


Least Squares
The least-squares method chooses the line that makes the residuals as small as possible overall. It does this by minimizing
\[
SSE = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2.
\]


Interpreting the Slope
The slope is usually the most important part of the regression equation. It tells us the predicted change in the response variable for a one-unit increase in the predictor.


Correlation and \(R^2\)
Correlation describes the strength and direction of a linear relationship. The coefficient of determination, \(R^2\), tells us the proportion of variation in the response explained by the fitted linear model.


Inference for the Slope
Regression inference allows us to test whether the predictor has a statistically meaningful linear relationship with the response. A common test is
\[
H_0:\beta_1=0
\qquad \text{versus} \qquad
H_A:\beta_1\ne 0.
\]


Prediction and Diagnostics
A fitted regression line can be used for prediction, but only after checking whether the model is reasonable. Residual plots help us detect curvature, changing spread, outliers, and other model issues.

title: Chapter 6: Hypothesis Tests
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of Chapter 6 you’ll be able to:

State null and alternative hypotheses for one-sided and two-sided tests.
Compute and interpret p-values using \(Z\), \(t\), \(\chi^2\), and \(F\) reference distributions.
Run one-sample tests for a population mean, proportion, and variance.

Recognize when paired data should be tested through differences.
Write conclusions in context without overclaiming what a p-value means.

title: Chapter 6: Hypothesis Tests
text:
Key ideas

Hypothesis Test Logic
A hypothesis test asks whether the observed sample statistic would be unusual if the null hypothesis were true. Small p-values give evidence against the null hypothesis.


P-Value Interpretation
The p-value is calculated assuming \(H_0\) is true. It is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true, and failing to reject \(H_0\) does not prove \(H_0\).


One-Sample Tests
Use a one-sample \(z\) test when \(\sigma\) is known, a one-sample \(t\) test when \(\sigma\) is unknown, a one-proportion \(z\) test for a population proportion, and a chi-square test for a population variance.


Two-Sample Tests
For independent groups, test differences such as \(\mu_1-\mu_2\) or \(p_1-p_2\). For paired data, first compute differences within each pair and then run a one-sample \(t\) test on \(\mu_d\).


Choosing the Right Reference Distribution
The reference distribution comes from the parameter and what is known: \(Z\) for known standard deviations or large-count proportion tests, \(t\) for unknown standard deviations, \(\chi^2\) for one variance, and \(F\) for a ratio of variances.

What you’ll learn
By the end of Chapter 5 you’ll be able to:

title: Chapter 5: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key ideas

Confidence Interval Skeleton
Most confidence intervals follow the same pattern: \[
\text{estimate} \pm
\left(\text{critical value}\right)
\left(\text{standard error}\right).
\] The critical value comes from a reference distribution such as \(Z\), \(t\), \(\chi^2\), or \(F\).


Interpretation
A 95% confidence interval does not mean there is a 95% probability that this particular interval contains the parameter. The parameter is fixed. Instead, the method captures the true parameter in about 95% of repeated samples.


One-Sample Intervals
Use a \(z\)-interval when estimating a mean with known \(\sigma\), a \(t\)-interval when \(\sigma\) is unknown, a normal approximation for a proportion when success-failure counts are large, and a chi-square interval for a variance when the population is normal.


Two-Sample Intervals
For independent groups, the target parameter is usually a difference: \(\mu_1-\mu_2\) or \(p_1-p_2\). For paired data, first compute differences within each pair, then build a one-sample \(t\)-interval for \(\mu_d\).


Planning Sample Size
To guarantee a margin of error \(E\), solve the margin-of-error formula for \(n\) and always round up. For proportions with no prior estimate, use the conservative planning value \(p^*=0.5\).

title: Chapter 2: An Introduction to R
text:
Key ideas

R vs RStudio
R is the engine that runs the calculations. RStudio is the dashboard you use to drive it. You install R first, then RStudio on top of it.


Scripts beat point-and-click
Writing analysis as code makes it reproducible, easy to share, and easy to re-run when the data changes. This is the single biggest reason statisticians use R.


R as a calculator
R handles + - * /, exponentiation ^, modulo %%, integer division %/%, and a full set of math functions (sqrt, log, exp, abs, round) and trig functions out of the box.


Data structures

Vectors — same-type values in one dimension
Lists — mixed types, any structure
Matrices / Arrays — same type, 2+ dimensions
Factors — categorical variables with named levels
Data frames — table of variables (columns) and observations (rows)



Functions and packages
Most R commands look like function_name(input). Packages extend R with new functions — install once with install.packages(), load each session with library().

3.1 Representing Data

Data and notation
Data are measurements we write symbolically. For \(n\) observations, we use a lowercase letter \(x\) with a subscript for the index:
\[x_1, \; x_2, \; \ldots, \; x_n\]
where \(x_i\) is one observation and \(i = 1, \ldots, n\). The value \(n\) is the sample size.

title: STA258
text:
3.2 Numerical Measures


Centre Where is the “typical” value? Mean, median, mode.


Spread How dispersed are the values? Variance, SD, range, IQR.


Position Where does one value sit relative to the rest? Percentiles, quartiles.




No single number tells the whole story. We pair centre with spread, and read both alongside a plot.

title: STA258
text:
3.2.1 Mean



Sample mean \(\bar{x}\)
For a sample \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\),
\[\bar{x} \; = \; \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i}{n} \; = \; \frac{x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n}{n}\]


The mean is the arithmetic average - the one most people mean when they say “average.”

title: STA258
text:
3.2.2 Median

Median
The middle value of a data set once the observations are sorted in ascending order.
Let \(x_{(1)}, x_{(2)}, \ldots, x_{(n)}\) be the sorted values. Then:

If \(n\) is odd: \(\;\;\) Median \(=\) observation \(\left(\dfrac{n+1}{2}\right)\)
If \(n\) is even: \(\;\;\) Median \(=\) average of observations \(\left(\dfrac{n}{2}\right)\) and \(\left(\dfrac{n}{2} + 1\right)\)

title: STA258
text:
Median in R













Sorted odd: 1, 1, 3, 4, 5 → middle value is 3.
Sorted even: 1, 1, 3, 4, 5, 9 → middle pair is 3 and 4, so median \(= (3 + 4)/2 = 3.5\).

title: STA258
text:
3.2.3 Mode



Mode
The most frequently occurring value in a data set.
A data set can have one mode (unimodal), two modes (bimodal), more than two modes (multimodal), or no mode if every value occurs equally often.

title: STA258
text:
3.2.4 Variance



Sample variance \(s^2\)
A measure of spread based on the squared deviations from the sample mean:
\[s^{2} \; = \; \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}\]
where \(\bar{x}\) is the sample mean.




Each term is squared, so \(s^2 \ge 0\) always.
The units of \(s^2\) are the units of the data squared (e.g. dollars²). That is awkward to interpret, which is why we usually report the standard deviation instead.

title: STA258
text:
Why divide by \(n-1\)?

Bessel’s correction. We use sample data \(\bar{x}\) to estimate the (unknown) population mean \(\mu\). That estimation step “uses up” one piece of information.
Dividing by \(n - 1\) instead of \(n\) corrects for this, and makes \(s^2\) an unbiased estimator of the population variance.


You will see a formal proof of this in STA260. For now, just remember:

Sample variance → divide by \(n - 1\)
Population variance → divide by \(N\)

title: STA258
text:
3.2.5 Standard Deviation



Sample standard deviation \(s\)
\[s \; = \; \sqrt{s^{2}}\]
where \(s^2\) is the sample variance.


Taking the square root returns us to the original units, which is why we usually report \(s\) rather than \(s^2\) in practice.

title: STA258
text:
3.2.6 Range



Range
\[\text{Range} \; = \; \max(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \; - \; \min(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\]
The difference between the largest and smallest observations.


Caution. The range uses only two values, so a single extreme observation can change it dramatically. It is a quick summary, not a robust one.

title: STA258

3.2.7 Percentiles

\(p^{\text{th}}\) percentile
In an ordered data set, the \(p^{\text{th}}\) percentile is a value at or below which approximately \(p\%\) of the observations fall.


Example. A class writes a difficult test and a student scores 72%. Although 72% is a B-, the test was hard. In fact, this mark sits at the 90th percentile for this test - approximately 90% of the class scored at or below 72%.
A relative position can matter more than the raw mark.

title: STA258
text:
3.2.8 Quartiles

Quartiles
Three values that split the sorted data into four equal-size groups.

First quartile \(Q_1\): 25% of values below it.
Second quartile \(Q_2\): 50% of values below it. This is the median.
Third quartile \(Q_3\): 75% of values below it.



Quartiles are just three specific percentiles: \(Q_1 = P_{25}\), \(Q_2 = P_{50}\), \(Q_3 = P_{75}\).

title: STA258
text:
Interquartile Range (IQR)



IQR
\[\text{IQR} \; = \; Q_3 - Q_1\]
The width of the middle 50% of the data.


Unlike the range, the IQR is resistant to outliers because it depends on \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) rather than directly using the minimum and maximum.

title: STA258

3.3 Graphical Techniques


Why plot at all? Numbers alone hide the shape of a distribution. A picture reveals skewness, gaps, clusters, and unusual values.


Two workhorses Histograms show the full shape of one variable. Boxplots highlight centre, spread, and outliers, and stack neatly for group comparisons.




Pair numbers with pictures. A mean of 65 looks different on a symmetric bell than on a right-skewed pile with a long tail. Always look at both.

title: STA258
text:
Skewness

Skewness
A measure of the symmetry (or lack of it) in the distribution of data.



Left-skewed Long tail on the left. Most values bunched on the right. Also called negatively skewed.


Symmetric Roughly mirror-image around the centre. Mean \(\approx\) median.


Right-skewed Long tail on the right. Most values bunched on the left. Also called positively skewed.

title: STA258
text:
Skewness Illustrated





The tail points in the direction of the skew. “Right-skewed” means the tail extends to the right. The mean is pulled toward the tail, while the median remains closer to the bulk of the data.

title: STA258
text:
Skewness vs Mean & Median



Rule of thumb

Left-skewed: Mean \(<\) Median
Symmetric: Mean \(\approx\) Median
Right-skewed: Mean \(>\) Median

The mean is generally pulled farther toward the long tail than the median.

title: STA258
text:
Outliers



Outlier
A data point that appears to lie outside the overall pattern of the rest of the data.


Do not just delete outliers.
Investigate first - is it a data-entry error, a measurement error, or a genuine rare observation? The right call depends on the cause.




Common causes

Transcription error (typing 100 instead of 10)
Measurement error (broken instrument)
A real but unusual case (a millionaire in a sample of incomes)

title: STA258
text:
3.3.1 Histograms

Histogram
A plot of a quantitative variable, built by:

Splitting the range of the data into intervals (bins).
Counting how many observations fall in each bin.
Drawing a bar over each bin with height equal to its frequency.

The \(x\)-axis shows the bins, and the \(y\)-axis shows frequency (or relative frequency).
Unlike a bar chart, the width of each histogram bar represents the width of its interval and therefore affects how the distribution is displayed.


Frequency vs relative frequency. Frequency histograms show raw counts; relative-frequency histograms show proportions (each bar height \(= f_i / F\), where \(F = \sum f_i\)).

title: STA258
text:
3.3.2 Boxplots

Boxplot (box-and-whisker plot)
A graphical summary based on quartiles, whiskers, and potential outliers:

Box spans from \(Q_1\) to \(Q_3\).
Line inside the box marks the median.
Whiskers extend out to the most extreme observation inside the outlier cutoffs.
Dots beyond the whiskers are flagged as potential outliers.

title: STA258
text:
The \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) Rule



Outlier cutoffs (fences)
\[\text{Lower cutoff} = Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\] \[\text{Upper cutoff} = Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\]
Any value outside these cutoffs is flagged as a potential outlier.




Example. A dataset has \(Q_1 = 5\), \(Q_3 = 11\), so \(\text{IQR} = 6\) and \(1.5 \times \text{IQR} = 9\).

Lower cutoff: \(5 - 9 = -4\)
Upper cutoff: \(11 + 9 = 20\)

Any value below \(-4\) or above \(20\) would be flagged.

text:
Boxplot in R

Where does the median sit inside the box? Off-centre suggests skew.
How long are the whiskers? Unequal whisker lengths also suggest skew.
Any dots? Those are potential outliers.

text:
Skewness from a Boxplot





Reading skew from a box. Median closer to \(Q_3\) with a long lower whisker suggests left skew. Median closer to \(Q_1\) with a long upper whisker suggests right skew. The longer tail points in the direction of the skew.

title: STA258
text:
9.1 Introduction to the Linear Model

A linear model has the form:
\[
y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1 x_{i1}+\beta_2 x_{i2}+\cdots+\beta_p x_{ip}+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i \sim N(0,\sigma^2).
\]
Here:

\(y_i\) is the response variable.
\(x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ip}\) are the predictors.
\(\varepsilon_i\) is random error.



The textbook model assumes predictors are fixed, errors are independent, and the errors have constant variance \(\sigma^2\).

title: STA258
text:
Simple Linear Regression

A simple linear regression model has exactly one predictor:
\[
y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2).
\]
The fitted regression line is:
\[
\hat{y}_i=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1x_i.
\]



Response
\[y\]
The outcome we want to explain or predict.


Predictor
\[x\]
The variable used to explain or predict the response.


Error
\[\varepsilon_i\]
The part of \(y_i\) not explained by the line.

title: STA258
text:
9.1.1 Least Squares Method

A residual is the difference between an observed data point and a fitted value from the regression model:
\[
e_i=y_i-\hat{y}_i.
\]
It is the vertical distance from the observed value to the fitted line.












If \(e_i>0\), the point is above the fitted line.
The model underpredicted the response.


If \(e_i<0\), the point is below the fitted line.
The model overpredicted the response.

title: STA258
text:
Sum of Squared Errors

For a fitted regression line, the sum of squared errors is:
\[
SSE=\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_i^2
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2.
\]
For simple linear regression:
\[
SSE=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(y_i-\hat{\beta}_0-\hat{\beta}_1x_i)^2.
\]


Least squares chooses \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\) to make \(SSE\) as small as possible.

title: STA258
text:
Least Squares Optimization

The least-squares problem for simple linear regression is:
\[
\min_{\beta_0,\beta_1}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2.
\]
The result is the fitted line:
\[
\hat{y}_i=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1x_i.
\]



The least-squares line is the best straight line according to squared residuals.


Least squares does not prove that a straight line is the right model.
It only finds the best line among straight lines.

title: STA258
text:
9.1.2 Estimating the Coefficients

For observed pairs \((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)\), the least-squares estimates are:
\[
\hat{\beta}_1=
\frac{
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})
}{
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2
}
=
\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},
\]
and
\[
\hat{\beta}_0=\bar{y}-\hat{\beta}_1\bar{x}.
\]


The fitted line always passes through the point \((\bar{x},\bar{y})\).

title: STA258
text:
Interpreting the Coefficients


Intercept
\[
\hat{\beta}_0
\]
The predicted value of \(y\) when \(x=0\).
Only interpret it if \(x=0\) makes sense in context.


Slope
\[
\hat{\beta}_1
\]
The predicted change in \(y\) for a one-unit increase in \(x\).
This is usually the main coefficient.



A slope is not just a number. It must be interpreted using the units of the predictor and response.

9.1.4 SSE, SSR, and SST

Regression separates the total variation in \(y\) into explained and unexplained pieces:
\[

SSR: variation explained by the regression line

\[

\]
Total variation.


SSR
\[

\]
Explained variation.

\[
\sum(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2
\]
Unexplained variation.

=

What it answers
How much of the response variation is explained by the straight-line model?


Connection to correlation
For simple linear regression with an intercept:
\[

\]

A large \(R^2\) does not prove causation.

9.2 Inference for Simple Linear Regression

For inference, we return to the model:
\[
y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2).
\]
The slope \(\beta_1\) is usually the main parameter of interest.



Main question
Does the mean response change linearly as (x) increases?


No relationship claim
\[
H_0:\beta_1=0
\]
The line has no linear slope.


Evidence
Use a confidence interval, a (t)-test, or an ANOVA (F)-test.



If \(\beta_1=0\), then the mean response does not change linearly as \(x\) increases. This is why slope inference is central in simple linear regression.

title: STA258
text:
9.2.1 Estimating Variance in Linear Regression

Because \(\sigma^2\) is unknown, we estimate it using the residuals:
\[
s^2=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_i^2}{n-2}
=
\frac{SSE}{n-2}.
\]
The denominator is \(n-2\) because simple linear regression estimates two parameters:
\[
\beta_0
\quad \text{and} \quad
\beta_1.
\]


The residual standard error is:
\[
s=\sqrt{\frac{SSE}{n-2}}.
\]
It measures the typical vertical size of the residuals.

title: STA258
text:
Standard Error of the Slope

The standard error of the least-squares slope is:
\[
SE(\hat{\beta}_1)
=
\frac{s}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2}}
=
\frac{s}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}.
\]
This estimates the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of \(\hat{\beta}_1\).


Larger spread in the \(x\) values gives a larger \(S_{xx}\), which makes the slope estimate more stable.

title: STA258
text:
9.2.2 Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Tests

A level \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for the true slope is:
\[
\hat{\beta}_1
\pm
t_{1-\alpha/2,\;n-2}
SE(\hat{\beta}_1).
\]
The reference distribution uses \(n-2\) degrees of freedom.



If the CI is entirely positive, the slope is plausibly positive.


If the CI is entirely negative, the slope is plausibly negative.



If the CI contains 0, then a zero population slope is plausible, so the data do not provide clear evidence of a linear relationship.

title: STA258
text:
Hypothesis Tests for the Slope

Common slope hypotheses are:
\[
H_0:\beta_1=0
\qquad \text{versus} \qquad
H_a:\beta_1\ne 0
\]
or one-sided alternatives:
\[
H_A:\beta_1>0
\qquad \text{or} \qquad
H_A:\beta_1<0.
\]
The test statistic is:
\[
t=
\frac{\hat{\beta}_1-0}{SE(\hat{\beta}_1)}
\sim t_{n-2}
\quad \text{under } H_0.
\]


A small p-value gives evidence of a linear relationship between \(x\) and \(y\).

\(y=\) new sign-ups in tens

Data:
\[
x: 1,\;2,\;3,\;4,\;5
\]
\[
y: 1,\;1,\;2,\;2,\;4
\]
Test whether the slope differs from 0.


Hypotheses
\[
H_0:\beta_1=0,
\qquad
H_A:\beta_1\ne0
\]
The reference distribution is \(t_3\).


Conclusion
Since the p-value is about 0.035, reject \(H_0\) at the 5% level.
There is evidence of a positive linear relationship.



Calculation
From least squares:
\(\hat y=-0.100+0.700x\), \(SSE=1.100\), \(S_{xx}=10.000\), \(n=5\).

1. Estimate the error variance
\(s^2=\dfrac{SSE}{n-2}=\dfrac{1.100}{5-2}=\dfrac{1.100}{3}=0.3667\)
\(s=\sqrt{0.3667}=0.6055\)

\(SE(\hat\beta_1)=\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}
=\dfrac{0.6055}{\sqrt{10}}
=0.1915\)

3. Test statistic
\(t=\dfrac{\hat\beta_1-0}{SE(\hat\beta_1)}
=\dfrac{0.700}{0.1915}
=3.656\)
\(df=n-2=5-2=3\)

4. Confidence interval for the slope
\(95\%\ CI:\ \hat\beta_1\pm t_{0.975,3}SE(\hat\beta_1)\)
\(=0.700\pm3.182(0.1915)\)
\(=(0.091,\;1.309)\)

Prediction, Interpolation, and Extrapolation

Once a fitted regression equation is available,
\[
\hat{y}=\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_1x,

9.2.4 Residual Plot Checks

Residual plot checklist


Random scatter: There should be no obvious pattern in the residuals.


No curve: A curved pattern suggests the relationship may not be linear.


Constant variance: The residuals should fall in a roughly horizontal band with similar spread.


No unexplained groups: Clusters may suggest that an important grouping variable is missing from the model.


No extreme residuals: Look for points unusually far above or below 0. A residual plot can flag unusual observations, but it does not by itself determine whether a point is influential.




Textbook logic
A residual-versus-fitted plot helps assess linearity, constant variance, and unusual observations. Normality and independence require separate checks.

Why Categorical Data Need a New Tool

So far, many methods focused on means, variances, or proportions.
In this chapter, the data are often counts across categories.
Examples:

Which app did a student choose?
Which colour did a customer prefer?
Which pickup time did an order fall into?
Which outcome happened in a repeated experiment?



The question is no longer “What is the average?”
The question is usually: Do the observed counts match what the model predicted?

title: STA258
text:
From Binomial to Chi-square



For two categories, one count can be modelled with a binomial distribution.
If \(Y_1 \sim Bin(n,p_1)\) and both \(np_1\) and \(n(1-p_1)\) are large enough, then
\[
Z=
\frac{Y_1-np_1}
{\sqrt{np_1(1-p_1)}}
\approx N(0,1)
\]
So,
\[
Z^2 \approx \chi^2_1
\]




Pearson’s idea
Instead of only checking one binomial count, compare every observed count to its expected count.
For two categories:
\[
Q_1=
\sum_{i=1}^{2}
\frac{(Y_i-np_i)^2}{np_i}
=
Z^2
\]
Therefore, \(Q_1\approx\chi^2_1\). This idea extends naturally to more than two categories.

title: STA258
text:
10.1 Multinomial Response Model

A multinomial response model applies when each trial results in exactly one of \(k\) mutually exclusive and exhaustive categories.
The category probabilities are:
\[
p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_k
\]
with
\[
p_1+p_2+\cdots+p_k=1
\]



Trials There are \(n\) independent trials with the same category probabilities.


Categories Each trial lands in one of \(k\) possible categories.


Counts The observed category counts are \(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots,Y_k\).

Goodness-of-Fit Test Statistic

The test statistic is:
\[
\chi^2
=
\sum
\frac{(\text{observed count}-\text{expected count})^2}
{\text{expected count}}
\]
where:
\[
\text{expected count}=np_i
\]
When all hypothesized category probabilities are specified before observing the data, the P-value is the area to the right of the observed \(\chi^2\) statistic under a chi-square distribution with:
\[
df=k-1
\]


This is always a right-tail test. Large \(\chi^2\) values mean the observed counts are too far from the hypothesized model.

10.3 Assumptions: Chi-sq goodness of fit

The chi-square approximation works well only when the expected counts are large enough.

\[
E_i=np_i\ge 5

Expected counts:

Problem situation
Expected counts:
\[
(2.5,4.5,18,25)
\]

\]
Large values give evidence against \(H_0\).




Final takeaway. A goodness-of-fit test turns a hypothesized probability model into expected counts \(E_i = np_i\), then uses \(\chi^2\) with \(df = k-1\) to judge whether the observed counts are close enough to the null model, provided each expected count is at least 5.

7.1 What Is Statistical Power?

Definition 7.1 The probability that a fixed-level significance test will reject \(H_0\) when a particular alternative value of the parameter is true is called the power of the test against that alternative.
\[\text{Power at }\theta=\theta_a
=P(\text{reject }H_0\mid \theta=\theta_a), \qquad 0\le \text{power}\le 1\]



High power (near 1) The test is good at detecting effects that are really there.


Low power (near 0) The test has a high chance of failing to detect the specific alternative effect being considered.

title: STA258
text:
What Affects Power?


1. Effect size  -  Larger gaps between reality and \(H_0\) are easier to detect \(\Rightarrow\) more power.


2. Sample size \(n\)  -  Larger samples shrink the standard error \(\Rightarrow\) more power.


3. Significance level \(\alpha\)  -  A larger \(\alpha\) makes \(H_0\) easier to reject \(\Rightarrow\) more power (but more Type I risk).


4. Variability \(\sigma\)  -  Less spread in the data \(\Rightarrow\) narrower sampling distribution \(\Rightarrow\) more power.


Researchers choose \(n\), \(\alpha\), and the smallest effect worth detecting. Variability is usually estimated from prior information, so sample size is often the main planning lever.

7.2 Type I and Type II Errors

A hypothesis test can reach the wrong conclusion in two ways.






\(H_0\) True
\(H_0\) False




Reject \(H_0\)
Type I (\(\alpha\))
Correct (power)


Fail to reject \(H_0\)
Correct
Type II (\(\beta\))






Type I error (\(\alpha\)) Reject \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is true.


Type II error (\(\beta\)) Fail to reject \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is false.



The consequences of Type I and Type II errors depend on the context. We choose \(\alpha\) in advance to control the probability of a Type I error when \(H_0\) is true.

The power of a test against an alternative is 1 minus the Type II error probability for that alternative:
\[\text{Power}=1-\beta = 1 - P(\text{Type II})\]




Reading the picture The orange tail under \(H_0\) is \(\alpha\). The red region under \(H_a\) is \(\beta\). Everything else under \(H_a\) is the power.

title: STA258
text:
Computing Power: The Recipe



1. Rejection rule in terms of the estimate. Convert the critical \(z\) (or \(z_\alpha\)) into a cutoff \(\bar{x}_*\) on the data scale using the null distribution.


2. Switch to the alternative. Assume the alternative value of the parameter is true.


3. Compute the rejection probability. Standardize the cutoff under the alternative and read off the area, which is the power.

title: STA258
text:
Example: A Better Espresso Blend



A specialty coffee roaster’s house espresso has scored a long-run average of 7.0 on a 10-point flavour scale. A new blend is developed, and the roaster will switch only if it truly scores higher. If the new blend’s true mean score is \(\mu=8.1\), will a 5% test reliably detect the improvement?
A panel of \(n=10\) trained graders scores the new blend; from years of calibration, grader scores have \(\sigma=1\).


\(\sigma\) is known \(\Rightarrow\) one-sample \(z\) test with reference distribution \(N(0,1)\).




Set-up
\[H_0:\mu = 7 \qquad H_a:\mu>7\]

\(n = 10,\quad \sigma = 1,\quad \alpha = 0.05\)
Detect the alternative \(\mu = 8.1\)

title: STA258
text:
Espresso: Cutoff to Power



Rejection Rule One-sided \(\alpha=0.05\) gives \(z_{\text{crit}}=1.645\). On the \(\bar{x}\) scale (since \(\sigma\) is known): \[\bar{x}_*=7+1.645\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\approx 7.520 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{reject if } \bar{x}>7.520\]


Find the Power Assume \(\mu=8.1\) is true and find \(P(\bar{x}>7.520)\): \[\text{power}=P\!\left(Z>\tfrac{7.520-8.1}{1/\sqrt{10}}\right)=P(Z>-1.83)=\mathbf{0.9664}\]












A 96.6% chance of correctly detecting \(\mu=8.1\). Since power \(=1-\beta\), the green and red areas add to 1: \[\text{power}=1-\beta=1-0.034=0.966\]

Example: Under-Dosed Medicine Vials


A pharmaceutical filling machine should dispense \(\mu_0=300\) mg of active drug per vial, with known \(\sigma=3\) mg from the validated assay. A routine quality check tests only \(n=6\) vials — will a 5% test catch a machine that has drifted to a true mean of \(\mu=299\) mg? \[H_0:\mu = 300 \qquad H_a:\mu<300 \qquad (\alpha=0.05)\]


\[\bar{x}_*=300-1.645\cdot\tfrac{3}{\sqrt6}=297.985 \quad(\text{reject if } \bar{x}<297.985)\] \[\text{power}=P\!\left(Z<\frac{297.985-299}{3/\sqrt6}\right)=P(Z<-0.83)=\mathbf{0.2033}\]


Only 20% power. With just 6 vials, this check will usually miss an under-dosing machine — the sample is too small.

Example: Monitoring a Server Room



A data centre keeps its server hall at \(\mu_0=22\)°C. Too hot and the servers overheat and fail; too cold and the cooling bill climbs for no benefit. Each day the monitoring system samples \(n=16\) sensor readings; from the sensors’ calibration, \(\sigma=2\)°C. If the cooling has truly drifted to \(\mu=23\)°C, how likely is the daily check to flag it?


A shift in either direction matters \(\Rightarrow\) two-sided test: \(\alpha\) splits into two tails of \(\alpha/2=0.025\) each, so \(z_{\alpha/2}=1.96\) and there are two cutoffs.




Set-up
\[H_0:\mu = 22 \qquad H_a:\mu \neq 22\]

\(n = 16,\quad \sigma = 2,\quad \alpha = 0.05\)
Detect the alternative \(\mu = 23\)
\(\sigma\) known \(\Rightarrow\) one-sample \(z\) test

title: STA258
section: Two-Sided: Two Cutoffs, Two Power Pieces
text:
Two-Sided: Two Cutoffs, Two Power Pieces


Rejection Rule Two cutoffs, using \(z_{\alpha/2}=1.96\): \[\bar{x}_*=22 \pm 1.96\cdot\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{16}} = 22 \pm 0.98\] \[\text{reject if } \bar{x}<21.02 \;\text{ or }\; \bar{x}>22.98\]


Find the Power Assume \(\mu=23\) is true; add the two rejection pieces: \[\begin{aligned}
\text{power} &= P(\bar{x}<21.02)+P(\bar{x}>22.98)\\
&= P(Z<-3.96)+P(Z>-0.04)\\
&\approx 0.000+0.516=\mathbf{0.516}
\end{aligned}\]

title: STA258
section: 7.3 Using Power to Determine Sample Size
text:
7.3 Using Power to Determine Sample Size


Too small Low power - real, meaningful effects are more likely to go undetected because the risk of a Type II error is higher.


Too large Wasteful - extra time, cost, and participants for precision you did not need.



Power analysis finds the minimum \(n\) that detects an effect of a given size with a specified probability (power), while holding the Type I rate at \(\alpha\).


To run it you must supply four ingredients: the standard deviation \(\sigma\), the significance level \(\alpha\), the target power, and the effect-size magnitude \(|\mu_a-\mu_0|\) you want to detect.

title: STA258
text:
The Sample-Size Idea



1. Cutoff from \(H_0\). The cutoff \(\bar{x}_*\) is the borderline value of the sample mean that decides whether you reject \(H_0\) or not. Write it using the null mean and the critical value \(z_\alpha\).


2. Cutoff from the target power. Write the same \(\bar{x}_*\) using the alternative mean and \(z_{\text{power}}\), the standard-normal quantile corresponding to the target power.


3. Set the two expressions equal and solve for \(n\). Round up to the next whole observation.



One-sided sample-size formula
\[
n=
\left(
\frac{(z_\alpha+z_{\text{power}})\sigma}
{|\mu_a-\mu_0|}
\right)^2
\]
where \(z_{\text{power}}\) is the standard-normal quantile corresponding to the target power.

title: STA258
section: Example: Detecting a Lift in Daily Active Minutes
text:
Example: Detecting a Lift in Daily Active Minutes


A product team’s app currently averages \(\mu_0=100\) daily active minutes. A new onboarding flow is believed to lift engagement. With \(\sigma=14\), they want power \(0.60\) to detect a true mean of \(\mu=103\). What is the smallest \(n\)? \[H_0:\mu=100 \qquad H_a:\mu>100 \qquad (\alpha=0.05)\]


Cutoff under \(H_0\) \(\;\bar{x}_*=100+1.645\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n}\)
Cutoff for power 0.60 \(\;P(Z>-0.25)\approx 0.60 \;\Rightarrow\; \bar{x}_*=103-0.25\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n}\)
Equate and solve \[100+1.645\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n}=103-0.25\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n}
\;\Rightarrow\; n=\left(\frac{(1.645+0.25)\cdot 14}{103-100}\right)^2\approx 78.2 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{n=79}\]

title: STA258
text:
Example: Vending-Machine Coffee


A campus vending machine advertises \(225\) ml cups (\(\sigma=7\) ml). You suspect it pours less. How many cups must you sample to reach power \(0.80\) against a true mean of \(\mu=223\) ml? (Target: \(P(Z<0.84)\approx0.80\), so \(z_{\text{power}}=0.84\).) \[H_0:\mu=225 \qquad H_a:\mu<225 \qquad (\alpha=0.05)\]


Equate the two cutoffs \(\;225-1.645\tfrac{7}{\sqrt n}=223+0.84\tfrac{7}{\sqrt n}\)
Solve for \(n\) \[n=\left(\frac{(1.645+0.84)\cdot 7}{225-223}\right)^2\approx 75.6 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{n=76}\]


Using the full normal quantiles gives \(n\approx 75.74\), so round up to 76 cups to obtain planned power of at least 0.80 against a 2 ml shortfall. The rounded values \(1.645\) and \(0.84\) give \(n\approx 75.6\) and the same final answer.

section: Power for a Proportion: Same Logic
text:
Power for a Proportion: Same Logic

For a one-sided test of \(p\), the rejection cutoff uses the null standard error, but power is computed with the alternative standard error:
\[\hat p^{\,*}=p_0 \mathbin{\substack{+\\[-4pt]-}} z_\alpha\sqrt{\tfrac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}, \qquad
\text{power}=P\!\left(\hat p \text{ in reject region}\;\middle|\; p=p_a\right)\]


Which sign on \(z_\alpha\)?









Test
Cutoff \(\hat p^{\,*}\)
Reject when




\(H_a:p<p_0\)
\(p_0-z_\alpha\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}\)
\(\hat p<\hat p^{\,*}\)


\(H_a:p>p_0\)
\(p_0+z_\alpha\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}\)
\(\hat p>\hat p^{\,*}\)






Three steps, same as the mean

Find the cutoff \(\hat p^{\,*}\) from \(p_0\) and \(z_\alpha\).
Standardize that cutoff under \(p=p_a\) using \(\text{SE}_a\).
The tail area past it is the power.

title: STA258
text:
General Power Formulas


Right-tailed, \(H_a:\mu>\mu_0\) \[\text{Power}(\mu_a)=\pi(\mu_a)=P\!\left[\,Z\ge z_\alpha+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\right]\]


Left-tailed, \(H_a:\mu<\mu_0\) \[\text{Power}(\mu_a)=\pi(\mu_a)=P\!\left[\,Z\le -z_\alpha+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\right]\]


Two-sided, \(H_a:\mu\ne\mu_0\) \[\text{Power}(\mu_a)=1-P\!\left[-z_{\alpha/2}+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\le Z\le z_{\alpha/2}+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\right]\]

Quantity

\(1-\beta(\theta_a)=P(\text{reject }H_0\mid\theta=\theta_a)\)

\(\alpha=P(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_0\text{ true})\)


Type II error

title: STA258
text:
Chapter Summary


Power Power is the probability of rejecting \(H_0\) at a specific alternative value, and it equals \(1-\beta\).


What Changes Power Power rises with a larger effect size, larger sample size, or larger \(\alpha\), and falls with greater variability.


Study Planning Choose a meaningful effect and target power, solve for the required sample size, and always round \(n\) up.




One-slide takeaway. A hypothesis test should be planned to have enough power to detect an effect that matters.

title: STA258
text:
8.1 Why ANOVA?


Purpose
Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) is used to compare several population means at once.
Instead of running many separate two-sample tests, ANOVA begins with one global test.



Question
Do all groups have the same population mean?
\[
k \ge 3
\]
groups are being compared.


Null hypothesis
The population means are all equal:
\[
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
\]


Alternative hypothesis
At least one population mean is different:
\[
H_a:\text{not all }\mu_i\text{ are equal}
\]



Key idea
ANOVA tells us whether there is evidence that at least one mean differs.
If ANOVA rejects (H_0), then pairwise comparisons can ask which means differ.

title: STA258
text:
One-Factor ANOVA Model


Textbook model
For observation \(j\) in group \(i\):
\[
Y_{ij}=\mu+\tau_i+\epsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2),
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\tau_i=0
\]
Here, \(Y_{ij}\) is the response value for observation \(j\) in group \(i\). The constraint \(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\tau_i=0\) makes \(\mu\) the overall population mean and uniquely defines the treatment effects.


Equivalent form
Since the population mean for group \(i\) is
\[
\mu_i=\mu+\tau_i,
\]
the same model can be written as
\[
Y_{ij}=\mu_i+\epsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)
\]


Meaning of the notation

\(\mu\): overall population mean
\(\tau_i\): treatment effect for group \(i\)
\(\epsilon_{ij}\): random error for observation \(j\) in group \(i\)
\(\mu_i=\mu+\tau_i\): population mean of group \(i\)



Intuition
Each observation is modeled as
\[
\text{response}
=
\text{group mean}
+
\text{random error}.
\]
So ANOVA asks whether all group means are equal:
\[
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
\]
or whether at least one group mean differs.

title: STA258
text:
ANOVA as a Prediction Problem


Main idea
ANOVA compares two prediction rules: one that ignores the group and one that uses the group.



Ignore group information
Predict every observation using the overall mean:
\[
\widehat X_{ij}=\bar X
\]
Total prediction error:
\[
SSTotal=
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}
(X_{ij}-\bar X)^2
\]
All observations are treated as coming from one common center.


Use group information
Predict observation \(j\) in group \(i\) using its group mean:
\[
\widehat X_{ij}=\bar X_i
\]
Remaining prediction error:
\[
SSE=
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}
(X_{ij}-\bar X_i)^2
\]
Each group is allowed to have its own center.



Improvement from using groups
The variation explained by group membership is the reduction in prediction error:
\[
SSTr=SSTotal-SSE
\]
If this improvement is large compared with the within-group error, the ANOVA (F) statistic becomes large.

title: STA258
text:
8.2 Sources of Variation

ANOVA works by splitting variation into two pieces: variation within groups and variation between groups.



Within groups: error variation
\[
SSE=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(n_i-1)S_i^2
\]
This is residual variation inside the groups.


Between groups: treatment variation
\[
SSTr=\sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i(\bar X_i-\bar X)^2
\]
This captures how group means differ from the overall mean.



The ANOVA \(F\) statistic becomes large when between-group variation is large relative to within-group error variation.

title: STA258
text:
Total Variation and Decomposition


Total variation
Total variation measures how far all observations are from the overall mean.
\[
SSTotal=
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}
(X_{ij}-\bar X)^2
\]


What ANOVA compares
ANOVA compares variation between group centers to variation inside the groups.
\[
\text{between-group variation}
\qquad \text{vs.} \qquad
\text{within-group variation}
\]


Decomposition identity
Total variation splits into treatment variation plus error variation:
\[
SSTotal=SSTr+SSE
\]


Intuition
If group means are close together, \(SSTr\) is small.
If at least one group mean is far away, \(SSTr\) becomes larger.


Big picture
ANOVA asks whether the between-group variation is large compared with the within-group error variation.

A mean square is a sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom:
\[
MS=\frac{SS}{df}
\]
So in one-way ANOVA:
\[
MSTr=\frac{SSTr}{k-1},
\qquad
MSE=\frac{SSE}{n-k}
\]


Degrees of freedom
The degrees of freedom split the same way as the sums of squares:
\[
n-1=(k-1)+(n-k)
\]
Treatment variation uses (k-1) df, and error variation uses (n-k) df.


Test statistic and p-value
The ANOVA test statistic is
\[
F^*=\frac{MSTr}{MSE}
\]
Under \(H_0\),
\[
F^*\sim F_{k-1,\;n-k}
\]
The p-value is the right-tail area.

Global ANOVA result
ANOVA tests whether all population means are equal:
\[
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
\qquad \text{vs.} \qquad

\]



Important limitation
Rejecting \(H_0\) tells us that not all means are equal.
It does not tell us which specific groups differ.


Follow-up question
After a significant ANOVA result, we ask:
\[
\text{Which means are different?}
\]


Pairwise comparisons
For three groups:
\[
\mu_1-\mu_2,\qquad
\mu_1-\mu_3,\qquad
\mu_2-\mu_3
\]
With \(k\) groups:
\[
m=\binom{k}{2}
\]

8.5 Pairwise Confidence Intervals


General idea
After ANOVA rejects, compare two population means using an interval for \(\mu_i-\mu_j\):

\[
(\bar{x}_i-\bar{x}_j)
\pm
t^*
\sqrt{
MSE\left(\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}\right)
}
\qquad
\text{where } \hat{\sigma}^2=MSE
\]




Fisher’s LSD
Use the ordinary two-sided critical value:
\[
t^*=t_{1-\alpha/2,\;n-k}
\]
This gives narrower intervals, so it has more power to detect differences.
It is less conservative when many pairs are compared.


Bonferroni
First count the number of pairwise comparisons:
\[
m=\binom{k}{2}
\]
Then use the adjusted critical value:
\[
t^*=t_{1-\alpha/(2m),\;n-k}
\]
This gives wider intervals.


Decision rule
A pair is declared different when the interval for \(\mu_i-\mu_j\) does not contain 0.
If the interval contains 0, the pair is not clearly different.
So the whole method is:
\[
\text{interval avoids }0
\Rightarrow
\text{different}
\]

title: STA258
text:
Bonferroni: Why Adjust?


The issue
After ANOVA rejects, we may compare many pairs of means.
Each pairwise comparison has a chance of making a Type I error, so doing many comparisons increases the chance of making at least one false discovery.



1. Count comparisons
With \(k\) groups, the number of pairwise comparisons is
\[
m=\binom{k}{2}.
\]
For example, if \(k=4\),
\[
m=\binom{4}{2}=6.
\]


2. Experiment-wise error
As the number of pairwise comparisons increases, the chance of making at least one Type I error across the full set also increases.
If the comparisons were independent, this probability would be
\[
1-(1-\alpha)^m.
\]
Bonferroni does not require independence.


3. Bonferroni correction
To keep the overall error rate controlled, Bonferroni uses a smaller per-comparison level:
\[
\frac{\alpha}{m}.
\]
For a two-sided interval, this gives
\[
t^*=t_{1-\alpha/(2m),\;n-k}.
\]



Key idea
Protected Fisher’s LSD is used only after the overall ANOVA rejects. It gives narrower intervals and more power, but its protection against familywise Type I error weakens as the number of groups and pairwise comparisons increases.
Bonferroni is more cautious: it uses wider intervals to control the familywise Type I error rate across all planned pairwise comparisons.

title: STA258
text:
5.1 Point Estimates and Interval Estimates


Point estimate
A single numerical value computed from sample data that serves as the best guess of an unknown population parameter.
Examples: \(\bar{x}\) estimates \(\mu\), \(s^2\) estimates \(\sigma^2\), and \(\hat p\) estimates \(p\).


Confidence interval
A plausible range of values for a population parameter, built from sample data and a specified confidence level.



Big idea. A statistic will usually not equal the parameter exactly. The interval tells us how far away the statistic could reasonably be.

title: STA258
text:
The CI Skeleton

Most confidence intervals (means, proportions, and their differences) follow the symmetric form:
\[
\text{estimate} \pm
\underbrace{(\text{critical value})(\text{standard error})}_{\text{margin of error}}
\]


Intervals for a variance \(\sigma^2\) follow their own skeleton — an asymmetric one built directly from the \(\chi^2\) distribution:
\[
\left(
\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\text{upper critical value}},\
\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\text{lower critical value}}
\right)
\]
Here, \(s^2\) is the point estimate of \(\sigma^2\), while \((n-1)s^2\) is the scaled sample variance used in the interval formula.



Estimate \(\bar{x}\), \(\hat p\), \(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2\), or \(\hat p_1-\hat p_2\).


Critical value From \(Z\) or \(t\), depending on the sampling distribution.


Standard error The standard deviation of the estimator, or an estimate of it.

title: STA258
text:
5.2 Interpreting Confidence



For a \(C\%\) confidence interval:
In repeated sampling, about \(C\%\) of intervals constructed using this method will capture the true parameter.


Do not say: “There is a 95% probability that this particular interval contains \(\mu\).”
The parameter is fixed. The random object is the interval produced by the sample.

title: STA258
text:
5.3.1.2 One Mean, Unknown \(\sigma\)

When \(\sigma\) is unknown, estimate it with \(s\) and use the Student \(t\) distribution:
\[
\bar{x} \pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\;n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt n}
\]



Why t? Replacing \(\sigma\) with \(s\) adds uncertainty. The \(t\) distribution has heavier tails, especially for small degrees of freedom.


Small samples For small \(n\), check that the population is reasonably normal or that the sample has no severe skew/outliers.

5.3.2 One Proportion

For a population proportion \(p\), with \(\hat p=x/n\):
\[
\hat p \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}

Random sample.


Independent Bernoulli trials.


Sufficiently large counts: \(n\hat p \ge 10\) and \(n(1-\hat p)\ge 10\).




Boundary check The final interval should make sense for a proportion. Values below 0 or above 1 need careful handling.

5.3.3 One Variance

For a normally distributed population, a confidence interval for \(\sigma^2\) is:
\[
\left(
\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,\;n-1}},

\]


This interval is asymmetric. Normality matters here much more than it does for large-sample mean intervals.

title: STA258
text:
5.4 Two-Sample Confidence Intervals











A two-sample confidence interval estimates a population quantity that compares two groups.
The groups must be clearly labelled, because the order matters. Changing the order changes the interpretation.


Mean and proportion differences: \(\text{Group 1}-\text{Group 2}\)


Variance ratios: \(\dfrac{\text{Group 1}}{\text{Group 2}}\)





Difference of means
\[
\mu_1-\mu_2
\]
Compares two population averages.


Difference of proportions
\[
p_1-p_2
\]
Compares two population percentages.


Ratio of variances
\[
\frac{\sigma_1^2}{\sigma_2^2}
\]
Compares two population variances.

title: STA258
section: 5.4.1 Confidence Interval for a Difference of Means
text:
5.4.1 Confidence Interval for a Difference of Means

For two independent populations, we often want to estimate:
\[
\mu_1-\mu_2
\]
A natural statistic is:
\[
\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2
\]



Case 1 \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) known
Use a \(z\) interval.
Rare in practice.


Case 2 \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) unknown, but assumed equal
Use a pooled two-sample \(t\) interval.


Case 3 \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) unknown and assumed unequal
Use Welch’s two-sample \(t\) interval.

section: Difference of Means: Equal Unknown Variances
text:
Difference of Means: Equal Unknown Variances

If \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) are unknown but assumed equal, we pool the two sample variances.
The pooled variance is:
\[
s_p^2 =
\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}
\]
The level \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu_1-\mu_2\) is:
\[
(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)
\pm
t_{1-\alpha/2,\;n_1+n_2-2}
s_p
\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}}
\]


Use this only when the equal-variance assumption is reasonable. Otherwise, use Welch’s interval.

title: STA258
section: Difference of Means: Unequal Unknown Variances
text:
Difference of Means: Unequal Unknown Variances

If the population variances are unknown and are assumed unequal, use Welch’s two-sample \(t\) interval:
\[
(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2)
\pm
t_{1-\alpha/2,\,df}
\sqrt{
\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}
+
\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}
}
\]
This estimates:
\[
\mu_1 - \mu_2
\]
when the two samples are independent and the equal-variance assumption is not reasonable.


Course note. Welch’s method is the more flexible default when the two sample variances look meaningfully different.

title: STA258
text:
Welch Degrees of Freedom

Degrees of freedom note
In this course, we are not testing your ability to be a calculator in an exam setting.
For hand calculations, you may use the conservative degrees of freedom:
\[
df = \min(n_1 - 1,\; n_2 - 1)
\]


A more accurate approximation, commonly used by software, is the Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom:
\[
df =
\frac{
\left(\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}\right)^2
}{
\frac{\left(s_1^2/n_1\right)^2}{n_1-1}
+
\frac{\left(s_2^2/n_2\right)^2}{n_2-1}
}
\]


How the examples use these methods
The upcoming Sports Highlight example uses the conservative rule \(df=\min(n_1-1,n_2-1)\) for a manageable hand calculation. The Food Delivery example uses the more accurate Welch–Satterthwaite approximation to illustrate the calculation used by statistical software.
For exams, use the conservative rule unless told otherwise.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Sports Highlight Watch-Time Comparison


A sports media team uses two independent random samples of viewers to compare watch times for two types of highlight playlists.
One playlist has shorter, fast-paced clips, while the other has longer, more detailed highlight clips.
Assume watch times are approximately normal within each population.

Group 1: Short-highlight viewers
\(n_1=24,\quad \bar{x}_1=9.8,\quad s_1=3.1\) minutes
Group 2: Long-highlight viewers
\(n_2=20,\quad \bar{x}_2=12.6,\quad s_2=5.8\) minutes
Construct a 95% CI for \(\mu_1-\mu_2\) using Welch’s method.


Calculation
\[
\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2
=
9.8-12.6
=
-2.8
\]
\[
SE=
\sqrt{
\frac{3.1^2}{24}
+
\frac{5.8^2}{20}
}
=
\sqrt{0.4004+1.6820}
=
1.4431
\]
Using degrees of freedom:
\[
df=\min(24-1,\;20-1)=19
\]
\[
-2.8\pm2.093(1.4431)
=
-2.8\pm3.02
\]
\[
(-5.82,\;0.22)
\]


Target parameter
We are estimating \(\mu_1-\mu_2\), where:
\(\mu_1=\) mean watch time for short-highlight viewers
\(\mu_2=\) mean watch time for long-highlight viewers
The order is short highlights minus long highlights.


We are 95% confident that the short-highlight playlist’s population mean watch time is between 5.82 minutes lower and 0.22 minutes higher than the long-highlight playlist’s population mean watch time. Since the interval crosses 0, the data do not show a clear difference in mean watch time.

text:
Example: Food Delivery vs Meal Prep Spending


A budgeting app wants to compare average weekly food spending for two types of young adults.
One group often orders from food delivery apps. The other group usually meal preps or cooks at home.
The sample standard deviations are noticeably different, so equal population variances are not assumed.

Group 1: Food delivery users
\(n_1=18\), \(\bar{x}_1=96\) dollars, \(s_1=22\)
Group 2: Meal prep users
\(n_2=22\), \(\bar{x}_2=82\) dollars, \(s_2=16\)


Calculation
\[
\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2=96-82=14
\]
\[
SE=
\sqrt{
\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}
+
\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}
}
=
\sqrt{
\frac{22^2}{18}
+
\frac{16^2}{22}
}
=
6.207
\]
\[
df\approx 30.3,
\qquad
t^*\approx1.697
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)\pm t^*SE
&=
14\pm1.697(6.207) \\
&=
(3.47,\;24.53)
\end{aligned}
\]


Target parameter
Construct a 90% confidence interval for \(\mu_1-\mu_2\).
The order is food delivery users minus meal prep users, so positive values mean food delivery users have the higher population mean weekly food spending.


We are 90% confident that food delivery users spend between 3.47 dollars and 24.53 dollars more per week on food, on average, than meal prep users.

title: STA258
text:
Assumptions for Two-Sample Mean Intervals

Assumptions


The two chosen samples should be independent and randomly selected, or come from a randomized experiment.


If both sample sizes are small, \(n_1<30\) and \(n_2<30\), then both populations should be approximately normal.


If only one sample size is small, then the smaller-sample population should be approximately normal.




CLT note
If both \(n_1\ge 30\) and \(n_2\ge 30\), the normality assumption is not required by the Central Limit Theorem.

A streaming app randomly assigns eligible free-trial users to one of two independent reminder groups before their trials end.
One group receives a direct reminder about the upcoming charge. The other group receives a general app notification.

Group 1: Direct reminder users
\(x_1=78\) of \(n_1=300\) continued the subscription
Group 2: General notification users
\(x_2=52\) of \(n_2=280\) continued the subscription


Calculation
\[
\hat p_1=\frac{78}{300}=0.2600,
\qquad
\hat p_2=\frac{52}{280}=0.1857
\]
\[
\hat p_1-\hat p_2
=
0.2600-0.1857
=
0.0743
\]
\[
SE=
\sqrt{
\frac{0.2600(0.7400)}{300}
+

}
=
0.0344
\]
\[

=
(0.0069,\;0.1417)
\]

=

+

0.0318
\]

=

Assumptions for Difference of Proportions

Assumptions


Randomization condition: The data in each group should be drawn independently and at random from a population, or generated by a completely randomized designed experiment.


10% condition: If the data are sampled without replacement, each sample should not exceed 10% of the target population. If a sample is bigger than 10% of the target population, random draws are no longer approximately independent.


Independent groups assumption: The two groups being compared must be independent from each other.


Large-count condition: Each group should have at least 10 observed successes and at least 10 observed failures: \(n_1\hat p_1 \ge 10\), \(n_1(1-\hat p_1)\ge 10\), \(n_2\hat p_2 \ge 10\), and \(n_2(1-\hat p_2)\ge 10\).




Practical reminder
Before interpreting the interval, clearly state the order of the groups. The difference \(p_1-p_2\) has the opposite interpretation from \(p_2-p_1\).

title: STA258
section: 5.4.3 Confidence Interval for a Ratio of Variances
text:
5.4.3 Confidence Interval for a Ratio of Variances

To compare two population variances, the parameter is:
\[
\frac{\sigma_1^2}{\sigma_2^2}
\]
If both populations are normal and the samples are independent, then:
\[
\frac{s_1^2/\sigma_1^2}{s_2^2/\sigma_2^2}
\sim
F_{n_1-1,\;n_2-1}
\]


A ratio near 1 suggests similar variances. A ratio far above or below 1 suggests one population is more variable.

title: STA258
text:
Ratio of Variances: Formula

A level \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\) is:
\[
\left(
\frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{1-\alpha/2,\;n_1-1,\;n_2-1}},
\;
\frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{\alpha/2,\;n_1-1,\;n_2-1}}
\right)
\]


This interval is sensitive to the normality assumption. For variance ratios, normality matters more than it does for large-sample mean intervals.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Sale Checkout-Time Variability


An online retailer wants to compare how inconsistent checkout times are during a regular purchase period versus a limited-time sale period.
Assume checkout times in both periods are approximately normal and that the two samples are independent random samples.

Group 1: Regular checkout period
\(n_1=18,\quad s_1=6\) minutes
Group 2: Limited-time sale checkout period
\(n_2=16,\quad s_2=14\) minutes
Construct a 95% confidence interval for:
\[
\frac{\sigma_2^2}{\sigma_1^2}
\]


Calculation
\[
F_{0.975,15,17}\approx2.723,
\qquad
F_{0.025,15,17}\approx0.356
\]
Using the unrounded critical values,
\[
\left(
\frac{5.4444}{F_{0.975,15,17}},
\frac{5.4444}{F_{0.025,15,17}}
\right)
\approx
(2.00,\;15.31)
\]


Target parameter
The order is limited-time sale checkout variability divided by regular checkout variability.
Values above 1 mean the limited-time sale checkout times are more variable.


We are 95% confident that the limited-time sale checkout-time variance is between 2.00 and 15.31 times the regular checkout-time variance. This suggests the sale checkout process is much less consistent.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Charging-Time Variability


A phone reviewer wants to compare how consistent two charging setups are.
Both setups are tested from 20% to 80% battery under similar conditions. The question is not which setup is faster on average, but which setup has more variability in charging time.
Assume the two datasets are independent random samples and that charging times are approximately normal within both populations.

Group 1: Budget fast charger
\(n_1=16\), \(s_1=12\) minutes
Group 2: Branded fast charger
\(n_2=14\), \(s_2=8\) minutes


Calculation
\[
\frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}
=
\frac{12^2}{8^2}
=
2.25
\]
\[
df_1=n_1-1=15,
\qquad
df_2=n_2-1=13
\]
\[
F_{0.975,15,13}=3.053,
\qquad
F_{0.025,15,13}=0.342
\]
\[
\left(
\frac{2.25}{3.053},
\frac{2.25}{0.342}
\right)
=
(0.74,\;6.58)
\]


Target parameter
Construct a 95% confidence interval for \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\).
The order is budget charger variance divided by branded charger variance, so values above 1 mean the budget charger has more variable charging times.


We are 95% confident that the budget charger’s population variance in charging time is between 0.74 and 6.58 times the branded charger’s population variance. Since 1 is inside the interval, equal variances are plausible.

Assumptions for Ratio of Variances

Assumptions


Independence: The two samples must be independent of each other.


Random sampling: Each sample should be obtained through a random selection process.


Normality: Both populations should be normally distributed. This is important because the ratio of sample variances follows an \(F\) distribution only when the underlying populations are normal.


Equal measurement scale: The two variables being compared should be measured on the same or comparable scales.




Important note
Violations of these assumptions, especially normality, can lead to inaccurate confidence intervals and invalid conclusions.

title: STA258
text:
5.5 Confidence Intervals on Paired Data

Paired data occur when observations are naturally matched.
Instead of comparing two independent sample means, we compute one difference for each pair:
\[
d_i=\text{first measurement}-\text{second measurement}
\]
or equivalently in the opposite order, as long as the order is clearly defined and used consistently.
We then build a one-sample \(t\) interval for the population mean difference \(\mu_d\).



Examples

Before and after measurements on the same person
Matched twins
The same student under two testing conditions
The same object measured by two devices



Do not treat paired data as two independent samples. The pairing is the main information.
Reversing the order of subtraction reverses the signs of the differences and the confidence-interval endpoints, so always interpret the interval using the stated order.

title: STA258
text:
Paired Data: Formula

Let \(d_1,d_2,\ldots,d_n\) be the paired differences.
The level \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu_d\) is:
\[
\bar{d}
\pm
t_{1-\alpha/2,\;n-1}
\frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
where \(\bar{d}\) is the sample mean of the differences and \(s_d\) is the sample standard deviation of the differences.


The normality condition applies to the differences, not necessarily to the original two measurements separately.

text:
Visual: Paired Data Means Differences







Each grey line connects the same person from before to after. The coloured dots identify the paired observations, and the labels show the within-person increase.

title: STA258
section: Example: Vitamin C and Sick Days
text:
Example: Vitamin C and Sick Days


A random sample of 12 people is observed during two comparable winter periods:

without regular Vitamin C
with regular Vitamin C

Assume the paired differences in sick days are approximately normally distributed.
For each person, define
\[
d=\text{sick days without Vitamin C}
-\text{sick days with Vitamin C}
\]
Observed differences:
\[
2,\;1,\;3,\;0,\;2,\;4,\;1,\;2,\;3,\;1,\;0,\;2
\]


Calculation
\[
n=12,
\qquad
\bar d=1.750,
\qquad
s_d=1.215
\]
\[
SE=
\frac{s_d}{\sqrt n}
=
\frac{1.215}{\sqrt{12}}
=
0.351
\]
\[
df=11,
\qquad
t^*=2.201
\]
\[
1.750\pm2.201(0.351)
=
(0.98,\;2.52)
\]


Order
Construct a 95% confidence interval for \(\mu_d\).
\[
d=\text{without Vitamin C}-\text{with Vitamin C}
\]
Positive values mean fewer sick days during the Vitamin C period.


Interpretation
We are 95% confident that the Vitamin C period had between 0.98 and 2.52 fewer sick days on average.
Because Vitamin C use was not randomly assigned, this shows an association, not proof of causation.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Phone-Free Bedtime Routine


A sleep app wants to study whether a phone-free bedtime routine is associated with more sleep.
A random sample of 12 people tracks their sleep before and after using a 30-minute phone-free routine before bed. Assume the paired differences are approximately normally distributed.
For each person, define:
\[
d=\text{sleep after routine}-\text{sleep before routine}
\]
Observed differences in minutes:
\[
18,\;12,\;24,\;9,\;30,\;15,\;21,\;6,\;27,\;12,\;18,\;24
\]


Calculation
\[
n=12,
\qquad
\bar d=18.000,
\qquad
s_d=7.459
\]
\[
SE=
\frac{s_d}{\sqrt n}
=
\frac{7.459}{\sqrt{12}}
=
2.153
\]
\[
df=n-1=11,
\qquad
t^*=1.796
\]
\[
\bar d\pm t^*SE
=
18.000\pm1.796(2.153)
=
(14.13,\;21.87)
\]


Target parameter
Construct a 90% confidence interval for \(\mu_d\).
The order is after routine minus before routine, so positive values mean more sleep after using the phone-free bedtime routine.


We are 90% confident that the phone-free bedtime routine is associated with between 14.13 and 21.87 more minutes of sleep, on average, for people like those in this paired study.

Assumptions for Paired Data

Assumptions


Paired observations: Each pair of values should come from the same unit or from meaningfully matched units.


Independence of pairs: The pairs themselves should be independent of each other.


Normality of differences: The distribution of the paired differences should be approximately normal, especially for small samples.


Random sampling: The sample of pairs should be obtained through a random process or a randomized design.




Important note
The normality condition applies to the differences, not to the original two measurements separately. For larger samples, this condition becomes less critical because of the Central Limit Theorem.

title: STA258
section: 5.6 Sample Size Selection Using Confidence Intervals
text:
5.6 Sample Size Selection Using Confidence Intervals

Sample size selection works backwards.
Instead of asking:

What margin of error do we get from this sample size?

we ask:

What sample size do we need to achieve this margin of error?




For a mean
The required sample size depends on:

confidence level
desired margin of error
population standard deviation, or an estimate of it



For a proportion
The required sample size depends on:

confidence level
desired margin of error
a planning value \(p_0\)

If no reliable prior estimate is available, use \(p_0=0.5\) for the most conservative sample size.

title: STA258
section: 5.6.1 Sample Size for a Mean When \(\sigma\) is Known
text:
5.6.1 Sample Size for a Mean When \(\sigma\) is Known

For a confidence interval on a population mean with known \(\sigma\):
\[
E = z_{1-\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
Solving for \(n\) gives:
\[
n =
\left(
\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}\sigma}{E}
\right)^2
\]


Always round up to the next whole number. Rounding down would make the margin of error too large.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Online Entry-Form Completion Time


A university is testing a new online entry form and wants to estimate the population mean time required to complete it.
From extensive historical system data, the population standard deviation of completion times is treated as known:
\[
\sigma=24\text{ seconds}
\]
The university wants a 95% confidence interval with margin of error no more than:
\[
E=5\text{ seconds}
\]
Find the required sample size.


Calculation
\[
n=
\left(
\frac{z^*\sigma}{E}
\right)^2
\]
\[
z^*=1.96,
\qquad
\sigma=24,
\qquad
E=5
\]
\[
n=
\left(
\frac{1.96(24)}{5}
\right)^2
\]
\[
n=88.5105
\]
\[
n=89
\]


Planning goal
Find the sample size needed for a 95% confidence interval for the population mean online entry-form completion time.
The margin of error should be no more than 5 seconds.


The university should observe at least 89 form completions to estimate the population mean completion time within 5 seconds at 95% confidence.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Pickup-Time Estimate Accuracy


A ride-share app wants to estimate its average pickup-time prediction error.
From past trip data, the population standard deviation of prediction error is treated as known:
\[
\sigma = 22.5 \text{ seconds}
\]
The app wants the margin of error to be at most:
\[
E = 2 \text{ seconds}
\]
Find the required sample size for 99% confidence.


Calculation
\[
n=
\left(
\frac{z^*\sigma}{E}
\right)^2
\]
\[
z^*=2.576,
\qquad
\sigma=22.5,
\qquad
E=2
\]
\[
n=
\left(
\frac{2.576(22.5)}{2}
\right)^2
\]
\[
n=839.8404
\]
\[
n=840
\]


Planning goal
Choose \(n\) so the confidence interval for the population mean prediction error has margin of error no more than 2 seconds.


The app should sample at least 840 trips to estimate the mean pickup-time prediction error within 2 seconds at 99% confidence.

title: STA258
section: Sample Size for a Mean When \(\sigma\) is Unknown
text:
Sample Size for a Mean When \(\sigma\) is Unknown

When \(\sigma\) is unknown, we use a preliminary estimate \(s\) from a pilot study or previous data.
A practical formula is:
\[
n =
\left(
\frac{t_{1-\alpha/2,\;n-1}s}{E}
\right)^2
\]
but the \(t\) critical value depends on \(n\), the quantity we are trying to find.


This is why an iterative approach is used:

Start with the \(z\) approximation.
Use that \(n\) to get a \(t\) critical value.
Recalculate \(n\).
Repeat until \(n\) stabilizes.
Round up.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Tutorial Video Rating Estimate




An online learning platform wants to estimate the mean rating students give to a new tutorial video.
Each student rates the video on a 0 to 100 scale.
Since \(\sigma\) is unknown, the platform uses a pilot study:
\[
s=14.5
\]
They want the margin of error to be at most:
\[
E=4
\]
Find the required sample size for 95% confidence.


Planning goal
We are planning a confidence interval for the population mean student rating.
Because \(\sigma\) is unknown, the pilot-study standard deviation \(s=14.5\) is used as the preliminary estimate.




Calculation
\[
n=
\left(
\frac{t^*s}{E}
\right)^2
\]
Start with the \(z\) approximation:
\[
n_0=
\left(
\frac{1.96(14.5)}{4}
\right)^2
=
50.48
\Rightarrow
51
\]
Then update using \(t\) critical values:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{Use } n & df & t^* & \text{New } n \\ \hline
51 & 50 & 2.009 & 53.04 \Rightarrow 54 \\
54 & 53 & 2.006 & 52.88 \Rightarrow 53 \\
53 & 52 & 2.007 & 52.93 \Rightarrow 53
\end{array}
\]
So the sample size stabilizes at:
\[
n=53
\]


The online learning platform should sample at least 53 students to estimate the mean tutorial-video rating within 4 points at 95% confidence.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Grocery-Delivery Fee Estimate



A consumer app wants to estimate the average extra cost from grocery delivery fees, service charges, and tips.
A pilot sample gives an estimated standard deviation of:
\[
s=16\text{ dollars}
\]
The app wants a 95% confidence interval with margin of error at most:
\[
E=10\text{ dollars}
\]
Since \(\sigma\) is unknown, use the iterative \(t\) approach.


Planning goal
Find the sample size needed for a 95% confidence interval for the population mean extra grocery-delivery cost.
Because \(\sigma\) is unknown, the pilot estimate \(s=16\) is used.




Calculation
Start with the \(z\) approximation:
\[
n_0=
\left\lceil
\left(\frac{1.960(16)}{10}\right)^2
\right\rceil
=
10
\]
Then update using \(t\) critical values:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{Use } n & df & t^* & \text{New } n \\ \hline
10 & 9  & 2.262 & 13.10 \Rightarrow 14 \\
14 & 13 & 2.160 & 11.94 \Rightarrow 12 \\
12 & 11 & 2.201 & 12.40 \Rightarrow 13 \\
13 & 12 & 2.179 & 12.16 \Rightarrow 13
\end{array}
\]
So the sample size stabilizes at:
\[
n=13
\]


The iteration stabilizes at 13, so the app should sample at least 13 grocery-delivery orders to keep the margin of error at most 10 dollars.

title: STA258
text:
5.6.2 Sample Size for a Proportion

For a confidence interval on a population proportion, the margin of error is approximately:
\[
E =
z_{1-\alpha/2}
\sqrt{
\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}
}
\]
Solving for \(n\) gives:
\[
n =
\left(
\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}}{E}
\right)^2
p_0(1-p_0)
\]


The value \(p_0\) is a planning value. If no prior information is available, use \(p_0=0.5\) because it gives the most conservative sample size.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Ad-Supported Plan Survey


A streaming service wants to estimate the proportion of subscribers who would switch to a cheaper ad-supported plan.
The company wants a 95% confidence interval with margin of error no more than:
\[
E=0.03
\]
There is no reliable prior estimate for the true proportion, so use the conservative planning value:
\[
p_0=0.5
\]


Calculation
\[
n=
\left(
\frac{z^*}{E}
\right)^2
p_0(1-p_0)
\]
\[
z^*=1.96,
\qquad
E=0.03,
\qquad
p_0=0.5
\]
\[
n=
\left(
\frac{1.96}{0.03}
\right)^2
(0.5)(0.5)
\]
\[
n=1067.11
\]
\[
n=1068
\]


Planning goal
Find the sample size needed for a 95% confidence interval for a population proportion.
The margin of error should be no more than 3 percentage points.


The streaming service should survey at least 1068 subscribers. We round up because rounding down would make the margin of error slightly larger than 3 percentage points.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Online Store Waitlist Survey


An online store is planning a limited product release for customers on a waitlist.
Before the release, the company wants to estimate the proportion of waitlist users who plan to make a purchase when it goes live.
A previous customer survey suggests a planning value of:
\[
p_0=0.156
\]
The company wants the margin of error to be at most:
\[
E=0.03
\]
Find the required sample size for 95% and 99% confidence.


Calculation
\[
n=
\left(
\frac{z^*}{E}
\right)^2
p_0(1-p_0)
\]
\[
p_0=0.156,
\qquad
1-p_0=0.844,
\qquad
E=0.03
\]
\[
n_{95}=
\left(
\frac{1.96}{0.03}
\right)^2
(0.156)(0.844)
=
562.0005
\Rightarrow
563
\]
\[
n_{99}=
\left(
\frac{2.576}{0.03}
\right)^2
(0.156)(0.844)
=
970.7698
\Rightarrow
971
\]


Planning goal
Find the sample size needed for a confidence interval for the population proportion of waitlist users who plan to make a purchase.
The margin of error should be no more than 3 percentage points.


The company should survey at least 563 waitlist users for 95% confidence and 971 waitlist users for 99% confidence. Higher confidence requires a larger sample size when the margin of error stays fixed.

Choose the correct interval

Identify the population parameter.
Decide whether the data involve one sample, two independent samples, or paired observations.
Determine whether the target is a mean, proportion, variance, or difference between parameters.
Select the appropriate reference distribution: \(Z\), \(t\), \(\chi^2\), or \(F\).



Report the result correctly

State the confidence level.
Include units when relevant.
Interpret the interval in the context of the population parameter.
Explain the meaning of 0 or 1 when interpreting differences or ratios.
Always round a required sample size up.





One-slide takeaway. A confidence interval combines a sample estimate with a measure of uncertainty to give a plausible range of values for an unknown population parameter.

title: STA258
text:
Why Uncertainty Is Built In

Two different samples of 100 UTM students will give two different sample means. So any estimate must come with a measure of how much it might be off.


This is where the tools in later chapters come from:

Confidence intervals - a range of plausible parameter values
Hypothesis tests - checking whether data support a specific claim
Statistical power - how likely we are to detect a real effect

title: STA258
text:
A Closer Look at Sampling
How you collect your sample determines whether inference is honest.

Simple random sample (SRS) - every unit has an equal chance of being chosen.


Systematic - every \(k\)-th unit from an ordered list (e.g., every 50th student).


Stratified - divide into groups, sample from each group.


Cluster - randomly pick whole groups, survey everyone inside.


Convenience / Voluntary response - whoever is easy to reach or chooses to respond. Usually biased.

title: STA258
text:
Bias: When Samples Lie

Bias - a systematic tendency for a sample to differ from the population in a particular direction.



Classic bias traps:

Selection bias - surveying gym-goers about exercise habits
Voluntary response - Instagram polls (only loud opinions answer)
Non-response bias - the people who skip the survey are different from those who answer
Coverage bias - your sampling frame misses parts of the population

title: STA258
text:
4.1 The Normal Distribution



Normal Distribution - \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\)
\[f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \cdot \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]
for \(-\infty < x < \infty\).
Parameters: mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2 > 0\).


Also called the Gaussian distribution, after Carl Friedrich Gauss (1809). It is symmetric and bell-shaped, completely characterized by \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\).

title: STA258
text:
4.1.1 The Standard Normal Distribution

Standard Normal - \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\)
\[f(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \cdot e^{-z^2/2}\]
A special case with \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma^2 = 1\). Denoted \(Z\).


Standardising. Any \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) can be converted:
\[Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \sim N(0,1)\]
This lets us use a single table (or pnorm()) for any normal distribution.

Recall: The Gamma Distribution

Gamma Distribution
A random variable \(X\) follows a Gamma distribution with shape \(\alpha>0\) and scale \(\beta>0\), written
\[
X\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta),
\qquad
f_X(x;\alpha,\beta)
=
\frac{x^{\alpha-1}e^{-x/\beta}}
{\Gamma(\alpha)\beta^\alpha},
\quad x>0.
\]
The Gamma function is
\[
\Gamma(\alpha)
=
\int_0^\infty t^{\alpha-1}e^{-t}\,dt.
\]


Why do we recall Gamma?
The chi-square distribution is the special case
\[
\chi_k^2
\sim
\operatorname{Gamma}\!\left(\frac{k}{2},2\right).
\]
We use this connection to introduce chi-square, but we will not study the Gamma distribution further in this chapter.

title: STA258
text:
4.1.2 The Chi-Square Distribution

Chi-Square Random Variable — \(X\sim\chi_k^2\)
If
\[
Z_1,Z_2,\ldots,Z_k
\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}N(0,1),
\qquad
X=\sum_{i=1}^{k}Z_i^2,
\]
then \(X\sim\chi_k^2\).
Its probability density function is
\[
f(x;k)
=
\frac{x^{k/2-1}e^{-x/2}}
{2^{k/2}\Gamma(k/2)},
\qquad x>0.
\]


The chi-square distribution takes non-negative values and is right-skewed. As \(k\) increases, it becomes more symmetric.
\[
E[X]=k,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X)=2k.
\]

4.1.3 The Student’s \(t\)-Distribution

Student’s \(t\) Distribution - \(T \sim t_\nu\)
If \(Z \sim N(0,1)\) and \(U \sim \chi^2_\nu\) are independent, then
\[T = \frac{Z}{\sqrt{U/\nu}} \sim t_\nu\]
The pdf is:
\[f_T(t;\nu) = \frac{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu+1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{\pi\nu}\,\Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu}{2}\right)} \left(1 + \frac{t^2}{\nu}\right)^{-\frac{\nu+1}{2}}, \quad -\infty < t < \infty\]


The \(t\)-distribution has heavier tails than the standard normal distribution. As the degrees of freedom increase,
\[
t_\nu \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1)
\qquad \text{as } \nu \to \infty.
\]
Therefore, the \(t\)-distribution becomes increasingly similar to the standard normal distribution for large \(\nu\).

4.1.4 The \(F\)-Distribution

\(F\) Random Variable — \(F\sim F_{\nu_1,\nu_2}\)
If \(U\sim\chi^2_{\nu_1}\) and \(V\sim\chi^2_{\nu_2}\) are independent, then
\[
F
=
\frac{U/\nu_1}{V/\nu_2}
\sim
F_{\nu_1,\nu_2}.
\]
The distribution has support \((0,\infty)\) and two degrees of freedom: numerator \(\nu_1\) and denominator \(\nu_2\).


Beta-function connection
The Beta function is
\[
B(a,b)
=
\int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt.
\]
For \(x>0\), the density of \(F\sim F_{\nu_1,\nu_2}\) is
\[
f_F(x)
=
\frac{
\left(\dfrac{\nu_1}{\nu_2}\right)^{\nu_1/2}
x^{\nu_1/2-1}
}{
B\!\left(\dfrac{\nu_1}{2},\dfrac{\nu_2}{2}\right)
\left(1+\dfrac{\nu_1}{\nu_2}x\right)^{(\nu_1+\nu_2)/2}
}.
\]
The \(F\)-distribution is used to compare variances and forms the basis of ANOVA.

4.2 Sampling Distributions

Sampling Distribution
The probability distribution of a statistic (such as \(\bar{X}\)) computed from all possible random samples of a given size \(n\) drawn from the same population.



Key idea. \(\bar{X}\) is not a fixed number - it is a random variable. Each new sample of size \(n\) gives a different value of \(\bar{X}\). The sampling distribution describes how those values vary.


Why it matters. Understanding the variability of \(\bar{X}\) from sample to sample is the foundation for confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.

title: STA258
text:
Sampling Distribution of \(\bar{X}\)

Distribution of the sample mean
Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be an i.i.d. random sample from a population with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). Then
\[
E[\bar{X}] = \mu
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\]
The standard error of \(\bar{X}\) is
\[
\operatorname{SE}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]

title: STA258
text:
4.3 The Central Limit Theorem

Central Limit Theorem (CLT)
Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\) be i.i.d. with \(E[X_i] = \mu\) and \(\text{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2 < \infty\). Then as \(n \to \infty\):
\[\frac{\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - \mu)}{\sigma} \;\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}\; N(0,1)\]
Equivalently, for large \(n\): \(\quad \bar{X}_n \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(\mu,\, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)\)


Remarkable. For i.i.d. observations from any parent distribution with finite variance—such as a uniform, exponential, or Poisson distribution—the shape of the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}_n\) approaches normal as \(n\) grows.

title: STA258
text:
CLT: What “Large \(n\)” Means in Practice


Symmetric distributions Even \(n = 10\)–\(15\) is often enough. The normal approximation kicks in quickly.


Moderately skewed \(n = 30\) is a common rule of thumb, but the required sample size depends on the amount of skewness and the presence of extreme observations.


Heavily skewed May need \(n = 50\)–\(100\) or more. The more extreme the skew, the larger \(n\) must be.




Practical consequence. For large \(n\), the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}_n\) is approximately normal even when the parent distribution is unknown or skewed. This normal approximation provides the basis for large-sample confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for \(\mu\).
