4.4 Law of Large Numbers

Law of Large Numbers
As the sample size increases, the sample average becomes increasingly likely to lie close to the population mean.


The results in this section explain why long-run sample averages provide reliable estimates of population means.

title: STA258
text:
4.4.1 Convergence in Probability

Convergence in Probability
A sequence \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) converges in probability to a constant \(c\) if, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\),
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}
P\!\left(|X_n-c|\leq\varepsilon\right)
=
1.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}
P\!\left(|X_n-c|>\varepsilon\right)
=
0.
\]
We write
\[
X_n\xrightarrow{p}c.
\]

title: STA258
text:
Chebyshev’s Inequality

Chebyshev’s Inequality
For any random variable \(X\) with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), and any \(k > 0\):
\[P(|X - \mu| \geq k) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{k^2}\]
Equivalently: \(P(|X - \mu| < k) \geq 1 - \dfrac{\sigma^2}{k^2}\)


No distributional assumption. Chebyshev’s inequality holds for any distribution with finite variance. It is the key tool in proving the WLLN.

title: STA258

4.4.2 Weak Law of Large Numbers

Weak Law of Large Numbers (WLLN)
Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) be i.i.d. with \(E[X_i] = \mu\) and \(\text{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2 < \infty\). Then for every \(\varepsilon > 0\):
\[
P\!\left(\left|\bar{X}_n-\mu\right|>\varepsilon\right)
\longrightarrow 0
\qquad \text{as } n\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Equivalently, we write:
\[
\bar{X}_n \xrightarrow{p} \mu.
\]


The WLLN does not say that \(\bar{X}_n\) eventually becomes exactly equal to \(\mu\). It says that, for any fixed tolerance \(\varepsilon\), the probability that \(\bar{X}_n\) lies more than \(\varepsilon\) away from \(\mu\) approaches zero as the sample size increases.

title: STA258
text:
Proof Sketch: WLLN via Chebyshev



Key steps

\(\text{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\)
Apply Chebyshev with \(k = \varepsilon\):

\[
P\!\left(|\bar{X}_n-\mu|\geq\varepsilon\right)
\leq
\frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}.
\]

Since

\[
P\!\left(|\bar{X}_n-\mu|>\varepsilon\right)
\leq
P\!\left(|\bar{X}_n-\mu|\geq\varepsilon\right),
\]
we have
\[
0
\leq
P\!\left(|\bar{X}_n-\mu|>\varepsilon\right)
\leq
\frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}.
\]

As \(n\to\infty\), the upper bound approaches \(0\). Therefore,

\[
P\!\left(|\bar{X}_n-\mu|>\varepsilon\right)
\longrightarrow 0.
\]
Hence \(\bar{X}_n\xrightarrow{p}\mu\). \(\square\)




What does the proof need?

Finite variance \(\sigma^2\)
Independence, so \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar{X}_n)=\sigma^2/n\)
Identical distributions, giving a common \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\)

The CLT is not required—Chebyshev’s inequality alone is sufficient.

title: STA258
text:
6.1 What a Hypothesis Test Does

High-Level Idea A hypothesis test uses sample evidence to determine whether there is enough evidence against a claim about a population parameter.



Null hypothesis, \(H_0\) The reference claim about the population parameter that is assumed true when calculating the test statistic and p-value.


Alternative hypothesis, \(H_a\) The competing claim supported when the sample provides sufficient evidence against \(H_0\).



The test is performed assuming \(H_0\) is true. The p-value measures how unusual the data are under that assumption.

title: STA258
text:
The Six-Step Procedure



1. Check assumptions. Verify the sampling or experimental design, independence, and any Normal or large-sample conditions required by the test.


2. Choose \(\alpha\). Set the significance level before making the decision.


3. State hypotheses. Use the correct population parameter.


4. Compute the statistic. Standardize the estimate with the correct standard error.


5. Find the p-value. Use the reference distribution and the tail area that matches \(H_a\).


6. Conclude. Compare the p-value with \(\alpha\) and write the conclusion in context.



The assumptions must be reasonable before using the stated reference distribution to calculate the test statistic and p-value.

title: STA258
text:
Choosing the Alternative


Left-tailed
\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\qquad
H_a:\theta<\theta_0
\]
Use when the research question asks whether the parameter decreased or is smaller.
The null may equivalently be written as \(H_0:\theta\ge\theta_0\).


Right-tailed
\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\qquad
H_a:\theta>\theta_0
\]
Use when the research question asks whether the parameter increased or is larger.
The null may equivalently be written as \(H_0:\theta\le\theta_0\).


Two-sided
\[
H_0:\theta=\theta_0
\qquad
H_a:\theta\ne\theta_0
\]
Use when the research question asks whether the parameter changed in either direction.



For a one-sided test, calculations use the boundary value \(\theta=\theta_0\). This is why the null is often written with equality even when the full null claim contains an inequality.

title: STA258
text:
P-Value Areas




Left-tailed: \(P(W \le w^*)\).


Right-tailed: \(P(W \ge w^*)\).


Two-tailed \(Z\) or \(t\): double the tail area beyond \(|w^*|\).


Two-tailed \(\chi^2\) or \(F\): add the relevant lower- and upper-tail areas because the distributions are asymmetric.





Use the two dropdowns at the top-right of the plot: first pick the type of test (\(Z\), \(t\), \(\chi^2\), or \(F\)), then pick the alternative (left-tailed, right-tailed, or two-tailed). Then drag the dotted line to move the observed test statistic — the shaded area and the p-value label below the plot update as you drag (for two-tailed \(Z\) and \(t\), the two boundaries move together).




\(W\) is the test statistic from the chosen reference distribution (Z, t, chi-square, or F), with observed value \(w^*\).

title: STA258
text:
Decision Rule



If p-value \(\le \alpha\) Reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a\).


If p-value \(> \alpha\) Fail to reject \(H_0\).



Careful language Failing to reject \(H_0\) does not prove \(H_0\). It only means the sample does not provide enough evidence against it at the chosen significance level.

title: STA258
text:
Reading Strength of Evidence





p-value range
Textbook language




\(\le 0.001\)
Very strong evidence against \(H_0\)


\(0.001\) to \(0.01\)
Strong evidence


\(0.01\) to \(0.05\)
Evidence


\(0.05\) to \(0.075\)
Some evidence


\(0.075\) to \(0.10\)
Slight evidence


\(>0.10\)
Little or no evidence against \(H_0\)





Statistical significance does not measure practical importance. Pair the p-value with an estimate or confidence interval.

title: STA258
section: 6.2.1 Hypothesis Tests on the Mean, \(\sigma\) Known
text:
6.2.1 Hypothesis Tests on the Mean, \(\sigma\) Known

For testing \(H_0:\mu=\mu_0\) when \(\sigma\) is known, use the test statistic
\[
z^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}
\]
which, under \(H_0\), follows the standard normal reference distribution \(Z\sim N(0,1)\).



Reference distribution \(z^*\sim N(0,1)\).


Use when Testing a population mean with known \(\sigma\) and an appropriate random/normal-or-large-sample setup.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Coffee Fill Volume



The cafe chain Second Cup advertises that a large iced latte is filled to a target of \(\mu_0=7.2\) oz of base. Customers complain the cups feel light, so quality control pulls a random sample of \(n=40\) cups.
From years of calibration records, the filling machine’s standard deviation is known: \(\sigma=1.1\) oz. The sample mean is \(\bar{x}=6.7\) oz.
Test whether the true mean fill volume has dropped below 7.2 oz at \(\alpha=0.05\).




What we are given

Target mean: \(\mu_0 = 7.2\) oz
Known SD: \(\sigma = 1.1\) oz
Sample: \(n = 40\), \(\bar{x} = 6.7\) oz
Significance level: \(\alpha = 0.05\)



Which test? \(\sigma\) is known, so this is a one-sample \(z\) test with reference distribution \(N(0,1)\).

title: STA258
text:
Coffee Example: Calculation



Hypotheses \[H_0:\mu=7.2 \qquad H_a:\mu<7.2 \quad (\alpha=0.05)\]
Test statistic \[z^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}=\frac{6.7-7.2}{1.1/\sqrt{40}}=-2.8748\]
p-value \[\text{p-value}=P(Z\le -2.8748)=0.00202\]















Decision \(0.00202 \le 0.05\), so reject \(H_0\).


Conclusion There is sufficient evidence that the mean fill volume is below 7.2 oz.

title: STA258
section: 6.2.2 Hypothesis Tests on the Mean, \(\sigma\) Unknown
text:
6.2.2 Hypothesis Tests on the Mean, \(\sigma\) Unknown

For testing \(H_0:\mu=\mu_0\) when \(\sigma\) is unknown, replace it with \(s\) and use the test statistic
\[
t^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}
\]
which, under \(H_0\), follows the Student \(t\) distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom.



Reference distribution \(t^*\sim t_{n-1}\).


Assumptions Random/independent observations; population normal or sample large enough for the \(t\) approximation.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Food Delivery ETA



The delivery app Uber Eats promises an average drop-off time of \(16.5\) minutes. Suspecting their orders usually take longer, a student randomly selects 12 of their recent orders and records the wait time (in minutes):
16.2, 18.4, 15.7, 19.1, 17.3, 16.9, 20.4, 18.2, 15.9, 17.6, 16.7, 19.8
Test whether the true mean delivery time is greater than the advertised 16.5 minutes.


\[H_0:\mu=16.5,\qquad H_a:\mu>16.5\] \(\sigma\) is unknown, so use a one-sample \(t\) test.




What we are given

Advertised mean: \(\mu_0 = 16.5\) min
Sample: \(n = 12\)
Sample mean: \(\bar{x} = 17.68\) min
Sample SD: \(s = 1.53\) min
Significance level: \(\alpha = 0.05\)



Which test? \(\sigma\) is unknown and estimated by \(s\), so use a one-sample \(t\) test with reference distribution \(t_{11}\).

title: STA258
text:
Food Delivery ETA: Calculation



Hypotheses \[H_0:\mu=16.5 \qquad H_a:\mu>16.5 \quad (\alpha=0.05)\]
Test statistic \[t^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}=\frac{17.68-16.5}{1.53/\sqrt{12}}=2.682\]
p-value \[\text{p-value}=P(T_{11}\ge 2.682)=0.0107\]















Decision \(0.0107 \le 0.05\), so reject \(H_0\).


Conclusion There is evidence that the student’s mean delivery time exceeds the advertised \(16.5\) minutes.

title: STA258
text:
6.2.3 Hypothesis Tests on a Proportion

For testing \(H_0:p=p_0\), use
\[
z^*=\frac{\hat p-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}},
\]
which follows the standard Normal reference distribution under \(H_0\).



Reference Distribution
\[
z^*\sim N(0,1)
\]
Use the Null Value
The standard error uses \(p_0\), not \(\hat p\).


Required Conditions

Use a random sample or randomized design.
Observations should be independent.
When sampling without replacement, ensure \(n\leq 0.10N\).

Large-Count Condition
Under \(H_0\), check
\[
np_0\geq 10
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
n(1-p_0)\geq 10.
\]

title: STA258
text:
Example: Reusable Cup Discount



Last year only \(10\%\) of students used the reusable-cup discount at a campus cafe. After a sustainability campaign, a fresh random survey finds \(x=68\) of \(n=520\) students bringing their own cup.
Is this evidence that the participation rate has increased above \(10\%\)?


\[H_0:p=0.10,\qquad H_a:p>0.10\]
\[\hat p=\frac{68}{520}=0.1308\]




What we are given

Null proportion: \(p_0 = 0.10\)
Sample: \(n = 520\), \(x = 68\)
Sample proportion: \(\hat p = 0.1308\)
Significance level: \(\alpha = 0.05\)



Which test? Since \(np_0 = 52\) and \(n(1-p_0) = 468\) are both \(\ge 10\), use a one-sample \(z\) test for a proportion with reference distribution \(N(0,1)\).

title: STA258
text:
Reusable Cup Discount: Calculation



Hypotheses \[H_0:p=0.10 \qquad H_a:p>0.10 \quad (\alpha=0.05)\]
Test statistic \[z^*=\frac{\hat p-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}=\frac{0.1308-0.10}{\sqrt{0.10\cdot 0.90/520}}=2.339\]
p-value \[\text{p-value}=P(Z\ge 2.339)=0.0097\]















Decision \(0.0097 \le 0.05\), so reject \(H_0\).


Conclusion There is evidence the participation rate has increased above \(10\%\).

title: STA258
text:
6.2.4 Hypothesis Tests on a Variance

For one normal population, test a variance using the chi-square statistic:
\[
\chi^{2*}=\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2}
\]



Reference distribution \(\chi^2\) with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom.


Important condition The population should be approximately normal. Variance tests are sensitive to non-normality.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Protein Scoop Consistency



A fitness brand claims its protein powder is dosed so precisely that scoop weights have standard deviation at most \(2.8\) g. A reviewer weighs a random sample of \(n=28\) scoops and finds \(s=3.4\) g.
Does this undermine the consistency claim? Use \(\alpha=0.05\) and assume scoop weights are normal.


\[H_0:\sigma^2\le 2.8^2,\qquad H_a:\sigma^2>2.8^2\]
For the test statistic, evaluate the null hypothesis at its boundary, \(\sigma_0^2=2.8^2\). A larger sample spread is evidence against the “at most 2.8 g” claim.




What we are given

Claimed SD: \(\sigma_0 = 2.8\) g, so \(\sigma_0^2 = 7.84\)
Sample: \(n = 28\), \(s = 3.4\) g
Degrees of freedom: \(df = n-1 = 27\)
Significance level: \(\alpha = 0.05\)



Which test? Testing a claim about a single variance (normal population), so use a one-sample \(\chi^2\) test with reference distribution \(\chi^2_{27}\).

title: STA258
text:
Protein Scoop Consistency: Calculation



Hypotheses \[H_0:\sigma^2\le 2.8^2 \qquad H_a:\sigma^2>2.8^2 \quad (\alpha=0.05)\]
Test statistic \[\chi^{2*}=\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2}=\frac{27\cdot 3.4^2}{2.8^2}=39.81\]
p-value \[\text{p-value}=P(\chi^2_{27}\ge 39.81)=0.0534\]















Decision \(0.0534 > 0.05\) (and \(39.81 < 40.11\)), so fail to reject \(H_0\).


Conclusion There is not enough evidence that the true SD of scoop weights exceeds \(2.8\) g.

title: STA258
text:
6.3 Two-Sample Test Targets








Target parameter
Typical question
Reference distribution




\(\mu_1-\mu_2\)
Are two population means different?
\(Z\) or \(t\)


\(p_1-p_2\)
Are two population proportions different?
\(Z\) or \(\chi^2\)


\(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\)
Are two population variances different?
\(F\)




These tests all compare two independent samples.

title: STA258
text:
6.3.1 Two Means, \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) Known

When both population standard deviations, \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\), are known, use the test statistic
\[
z^*=\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1+\sigma_2^2/n_2}}
\]
which, under \(H_0\), follows the standard normal reference distribution \(Z\sim N(0,1)\).



Reference distribution \(z^*\sim N(0,1)\).


Use when Comparing two population means from independent samples with known \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\). Usually \(D_0=0\).

title: STA258
text:
Assumptions: Two Independent Means


Sampling structure


The two samples are independent.


Each sample is random, or the data come from a randomized design.


If sampling without replacement, each sample is less than 10% of its population.




Model condition


Each population is approximately normal, or both sample sizes are large enough for the CLT.


For a pooled test, equal population variances should be reasonable.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Comparing Download Speeds

Two campus internet providers both advertise fast service. From years of monitoring, download speeds (Mbps) are known to have \(\sigma_A=12\) for Provider A and \(\sigma_B=15\) for Provider B.
A student runs independent speed tests at randomly selected times under comparable campus conditions and records:

Provider A: \(n_A=40\), \(\bar{x}_A=86\) Mbps
Provider B: \(n_B=45\), \(\bar{x}_B=79\) Mbps

Is Provider A’s mean download speed higher than Provider B’s?


Let \(\mu_A\) and \(\mu_B\) be the population mean download speeds under these campus testing conditions. Test \(H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0\) against \(H_a:\mu_A-\mu_B>0\).
Both population SDs are known, so use a two-sample \(z\) test.

title: STA258
text:
Download Speeds: Calculation



Hypotheses \[H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0 \qquad H_a:\mu_A-\mu_B>0 \quad (\alpha=0.05)\]
Test statistic \[z^*=\frac{(\bar{x}_A-\bar{x}_B)-0}{\sqrt{\sigma_A^2/n_A+\sigma_B^2/n_B}}=\frac{86-79}{\sqrt{12^2/40+15^2/45}}=2.387\]
p-value \[\text{p-value}=P(Z\ge 2.387)=0.0085\]















Decision \(0.0085 \le 0.05\), so reject \(H_0\).


Conclusion There is evidence Provider A’s mean download speed is higher than Provider B’s.

title: STA258
text:
Check in R: Download Speeds









The output gives \(z^*=2.39\) and p-value \(0.0085\). At \(\alpha=0.05\), reject \(H_0\).

title: STA258
text:
6.3.2 Two Means, Equal Unknown Variances

When the population variances are unknown but can be assumed equal, pool the two sample variances into one estimate:
\[
s_p^2=\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2},
\qquad
t^*=\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}{s_p\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n_1}+\dfrac{1}{n_2}}}
\]



Degrees of freedom \(df=n_1+n_2-2\) under the equal-variance model. Welch’s test instead uses an estimated degrees of freedom.


When to pool Reasonable when the sample spreads are similar — e.g. the fold rule \(\dfrac{\max(s_1,s_2)}{\min(s_1,s_2)}<\sqrt{2}\).

title: STA258
text:
Example: Two Fertilizers, Similar Spread

A gardener randomly assigns independent tomato plots to one of two organic fertilizers and expects the two groups to have similar variability. The resulting yields (kg per plant) are:
Fertilizer A: 4.2 3.8 4.5 4.0 3.9 4.3 4.1 3.7 4.4
Fertilizer B: 3.6 3.9 3.4 3.8 3.5 3.7 3.3 4.0 3.6 3.5
Do the two fertilizers give different mean yields at \(\alpha=0.05\)?


Let \(\mu_A,\mu_B\) be the true mean yields. Test \(H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0\) against \(H_a:\mu_A-\mu_B\neq 0\).
Variances are unknown but the spreads look similar, so use a pooled two-sample \(t\) test.

title: STA258
text:
Two Fertilizers: Calculation



Hypotheses \[H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0 \qquad H_a:\mu_A-\mu_B\neq 0 \quad (\alpha=0.05)\]
Pooled variance \[s_p^2=\frac{(n_A-1)s_A^2+(n_B-1)s_B^2}{n_A+n_B-2}=\frac{8(0.274^2)+9(0.221^2)}{17}=0.0612\]
Test statistic \[t^*=\frac{\bar{x}_A-\bar{x}_B}{s_p\sqrt{1/n_A+1/n_B}}=\frac{4.10-3.63}{0.2475\sqrt{1/9+1/10}}=4.13\]
p-value \[\text{p-value}=2\,P(T_{17}\ge 4.13)=0.0007\]















Decision \(0.0007 \le 0.05\), so reject \(H_0\).


Conclusion There is strong evidence the two fertilizers give different mean yields.

text:

The output gives \(t^*=4.13\), \(df=17\), and p-value \(0.0007\). At \(\alpha=0.05\), reject \(H_0\).

title: STA258
section: 6.3.3 Two Means, Unequal or Unspecified Variances
text:
6.3.3 Two Means, Unequal or Unspecified Variances

For unequal or unspecified population variances, use Welch’s two-sample \(t\) test (no pooling), with test statistic
\[
t^*=\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}
\]
which, under \(H_0\), approximately follows a \(t\) reference distribution with the Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.



Reference distribution \(T\sim t_\nu\), with the Welch–Satterthwaite \(\nu\).


Use when Comparing two population means from independent samples when equal variances are not clearly justified.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Active Recall vs Rereading

Twenty-two students are randomly assigned to prepare for the same quiz using either active recall (self-testing) or passive rereading.
Active recall: 88 84 90 86 89 85 88 83 90 86 89 85
Rereading: 84 86 83 85 84 82 87 84 86 85
Does active recall produce a higher mean quiz score?


Let \(\mu_1\) be the active-recall mean and \(\mu_2\) the rereading mean. Test \(H_0:\mu_1-\mu_2=0\) against \(H_a:\mu_1-\mu_2>0\).

title: STA258
text:
Active Recall vs Rereading: Calculation



Hypotheses \[H_0:\mu_1-\mu_2=0 \qquad H_a:\mu_1-\mu_2>0 \quad (\alpha=0.05)\]
Test statistic (no pooling) \[t^*=\frac{\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}=\frac{86.92-84.60}{\sqrt{2.392^2/12+1.506^2/10}}=2.76\]
p-value \[\text{p-value}=P(T_\nu\ge 2.76)=0.0062,\qquad \nu\approx 18.8\]















Decision \(0.0062 \le 0.05\), so reject \(H_0\).


Conclusion There is evidence active recall produces a higher mean quiz score than rereading.

text:

Welch’s test reports \(t^*=2.76\) with \(\nu\approx 18.8\) and p-value \(0.0062\). At \(\alpha=0.05\), reject \(H_0\).

title: STA258
text:
6.3.4 Hypothesis Tests on Two Proportions

When testing \(H_0:p_1-p_2=0\), pool the sample proportions under the null and use the test statistic
\[
\hat p=\frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2},
\qquad
z^*=\frac{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}{\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}
\]
which, under \(H_0\), follows the standard normal reference distribution \(Z\sim N(0,1)\).



Reference distribution \(z^*\sim N(0,1)\).


Use when Comparing two population proportions from independent samples, with enough successes and failures in each group.

title: STA258
text:
Assumptions: Difference of Proportions


Sampling structure


The two groups are independent.


Each sample is random, or the data come from a randomized design.


If sampling without replacement, each sample should be less than 10% of its population.




Large-count condition under \(H_0\)
For testing \(H_0:p_1=p_2\), first calculate the pooled proportion:
\[
\hat p=\frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2}.
\]
Then check the expected successes and failures in both groups:
\[
n_i\hat p\ge 10
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
n_i(1-\hat p)\ge 10,
\qquad i=1,2.
\]

title: STA258
text:
Example: Push Notifications

A habit-tracking app runs an experiment by randomly assigning half of its new users to receive a daily push notification and the other half to receive none. For each user, the app records whether they completed a workout that day.
Push notification: \(142\) check-ins out of \(360\) users
No notification: \(118\) check-ins out of \(370\) users
Test whether the daily push notification increases the check-in rate.


\[
H_0:p_1-p_2=0,\qquad H_a:p_1-p_2>0
\]

title: STA258
text:
Push Notifications: Calculation



Hypotheses \[H_0:p_1-p_2=0 \qquad H_a:p_1-p_2>0 \quad (\alpha=0.05)\]
Sample and pooled proportions \[\hat p_1=\tfrac{142}{360}=0.394,\quad \hat p_2=\tfrac{118}{370}=0.319,\quad \hat p=\tfrac{142+118}{360+370}=0.356\]
Test statistic \[z^*=\frac{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}{\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}=\frac{0.0756}{0.0354}=2.13\]
p-value \[\text{p-value}=P(Z\ge 2.13)=0.0166\]















Decision \(0.0166 \le 0.05\), so reject \(H_0\).


Conclusion There is evidence the daily push notification increases the check-in rate.

title: STA258
text:

title: STA258
text:
6.3.5 Hypothesis Tests on Two Variances

For two normal populations, test a ratio of variances with the test statistic
\[
F^*=\frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}
\]
which, under \(H_0\), follows an \(F\) reference distribution with \(n_1-1\) and \(n_2-1\) degrees of freedom.



Reference distribution \(F^*\sim F_{n_1-1,\,n_2-1}\).


Use when Comparing two population variances from independent normal samples; the \(F\) test is sensitive to non-normality.

title: STA258
text:
Assumptions: Ratio of Variances


Required structure


The two samples are independent.


Each sample comes from a random process or randomized design.




Normality matters here


The \(F\) test for a variance ratio is sensitive to non-normality.


This condition is more important here than it is for many mean-based tests.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Scoring Consistency



Two basketball players average about the same points per game, but a scout suspects Player A is less consistent — more variable game to game.
Player A: 76 87 74 86 81 83 77 88 79 84 75 82
Player B: 82 84 79 85 81 83 80 86 82 84
Test whether Player A has the larger scoring variance at \(\alpha=0.05\).


\[H_0:\sigma_A^2=\sigma_B^2,\qquad H_a:\sigma_A^2>\sigma_B^2\]
\[F^*=\frac{s_A^2}{s_B^2}\sim F_{n_A-1,\,n_B-1}\]




What we are given

Player A: \(n_A = 12\), \(s_A^2 = 23.09\)
Player B: \(n_B = 10\), \(s_B^2 = 4.933\)
Degrees of freedom: \(df = (11,\ 9)\)
Significance level: \(\alpha = 0.05\)



Which test? Comparing two population variances from normal populations, so use an \(F\) test. Because the alternative is \(H_a:\sigma_A^2>\sigma_B^2\), Player A is placed in the numerator:
\[F^*=\frac{s_A^2}{s_B^2}\sim F_{11,\,9}.\]

title: STA258
text:
Scoring Consistency: Calculation



Hypotheses \[H_0:\sigma_A^2=\sigma_B^2 \qquad H_a:\sigma_A^2>\sigma_B^2 \quad (\alpha=0.05)\]
Test statistic \[F^*=\frac{s_A^2}{s_B^2}=\frac{23.09}{4.933}=4.68\]
p-value \[\text{p-value}=P(F_{11,9}\ge 4.68)=0.014\]















Decision \(0.014 \le 0.05\) (and \(4.68 > 3.10\)), so reject \(H_0\).


Conclusion There is strong evidence Player A has the larger scoring variance (i.e. is less consistent).

text:

title: STA258
text:
6.4 Paired Data

For matched pairs or before-after data, reduce each pair to a difference (measurement 1 \(-\) measurement 2):
\[
d_i = m_{1i}-m_{2i} \quad (\text{or } m_{2i}-m_{1i})
\]
Then run a one-sample \(t\) test on \(\mu_d\).



Not independent groups The two measurements inside a pair are linked.


Reference distribution \(t\) with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom for the differences.

title: STA258
text:
Assumptions: Paired Data


Paired structure


Each pair comes from the same unit, matched units, or a before-after measurement.


Analyze the differences \(d_i\), not the two original columns separately.


The pairs themselves must be independent of one another.




Sampling and model conditions


The pairs should come from a random sample or randomized experiment.


If sampling without replacement, the number of pairs should not exceed \(10\%\) of the population.


For a small sample, the distribution of the differences should be approximately normal.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Pomodoro Focus Timer

Each of 12 students completes a timed practice set, then writes a comparable set after a week of studying with the Pomodoro technique (25-minute focus blocks). Scores are paired within each student.
Before: 34 29 41 38 36 33 40 31 37 35 39 32
After: 37 28 45 39 38 33 38 34 38 39 41 33
Is there evidence that the students’ mean score is higher after the week of Pomodoro study than before?


Use paired differences \(d_i=\text{after}_i-\text{before}_i\) and test \(H_0:\mu_d=0\) against \(H_a:\mu_d>0\).

title: STA258
text:
Pomodoro: Difference Table


Reduce each pair (\(M_1\) = before, \(M_2\) = after) to \(d_i = M_2 - M_1\), then analyze the 12 differences as one sample.

What you’ll learn
By the end of Chapter 3 you’ll be able to:

Compute and interpret the mean, median, and mode as measures of centre.

title: Chapter 3: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Key ideas

Centre
The mean uses every value and is sensitive to extremes. The median is the middle value and is resistant to outliers. The mode is the most frequent value.


Spread
The range is max minus min — quick but easily distorted by one extreme value. The standard deviation \(s\) is the typical distance from \(\bar{x}\). The IQR \(= Q_3 - Q_1\) is the width of the middle 50% of the data and is resistant to outliers.


Why divide by \(n-1\) for the sample variance?
We use \(\bar{x}\) to estimate the population mean \(\mu\), which costs us one piece of information. Dividing by \(n-1\) corrects for that and makes \(s^2\) an unbiased estimator of the population variance. (Bessel’s correction.)


Position
The \(p^{\text{th}}\) percentile is the value such that \(p\%\) of observations lie below it. Quartiles \(Q_1, Q_2, Q_3\) split the sorted data into four equal-size groups — \(Q_2\) is just the median.


Shape and outliers
A histogram shows the full shape of one variable. A boxplot highlights the five-number summary and flags potential outliers using the \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) rule. The longer tail / whisker points in the direction of the skew.


Pair numbers with pictures
A single number rarely tells the whole story. Always report a summary statistic alongside a plot so the shape of the distribution is visible.

What you’ll learn

title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text:
Key ideas

Statistics in one sentence
The science of learning from data under uncertainty — moving from what we measured to what we want to know.


Population vs Sample
A population is the full group we want to learn about. A sample is the subset we actually measure. We use the sample to make claims about the population.


Parameter vs Statistic
A parameter (e.g. \(\mu\), \(p\), \(\sigma\)) summarizes the population — usually unknown. A statistic (e.g. \(\bar{x}\), \(\hat{p}\), \(s\)) summarizes the sample — known, and used to estimate the parameter.


Types of Data
Quantitative data are numeric: discrete (counts) or continuous (measured). Qualitative data are categorical: nominal (no order) or ordinal (ordered).


Inference
We collect a sample, calculate a statistic, and use it to estimate an unknown population parameter — always with a measure of uncertainty. This sets up confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, and the rest of the course.

title: Chapter 4: Foundations of Inference
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of Chapter 4 you’ll be able to:

Describe the Normal, Chi-Square, t, and F distributions and identify when each is used.
Explain what a sampling distribution is and why it is important in statistical inference.
Find the mean and standard error of the sample mean \(\bar{X}\).
Apply the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) to approximate the distribution of sample means.
Understand convergence in probability and interpret the notation \(X_n \overset{p}{\to} c\).
State and apply the Weak Law of Large Numbers (WLLN) to explain why sample averages approach the population mean.

title: Chapter 4: Foundations of Inference
text:
Key ideas

Normal Distribution
The normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, written as \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\). The standard normal distribution is the special case \(Z \sim N(0,1)\) and serves as the foundation for many inference procedures.


Chi-Square, (t), and (F) Distributions
The chi-square distribution \(\chi^2_k\) arises from sums of squared standard normal variables. The (t)-distribution \(t_\nu\) is used when the population standard deviation is unknown. The (F)-distribution \(F_{\nu_1,\nu_2}\) is commonly used for comparing variances and in ANOVA.


Distribution Tools in R
Use pnorm and qnorm for normal probabilities and critical values, pchisq and qchisq for chi-square calculations, pt and qt for (t)-distributions, and pf and qf for (F)-distributions.


Central Limit Theorem (CLT)
For large sample sizes, the standardized sample mean is approximately normal: \[
\frac{\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n-\mu)}{\sigma}
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,1).
\] This result allows normal-based inference even when the original population is not normal.


Convergence in Probability
The notation \[
X_n \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} c
\] means that as \(n\) grows, the probability that \(X_n\) differs substantially from \(c\) approaches zero.


Weak Law of Large Numbers
The sample mean converges in probability to the population mean: \[
\bar{X}_n \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} \mu.
\] As the sample size increases, sample averages become increasingly stable around the true mean. A proof can be obtained using Chebyshev’s inequality.

title: Chapter 7: Statistical Power
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of Chapter 7 you’ll be able to:

Define the power of a test and explain what makes power high or low.
Distinguish Type I (\(\alpha\)) and Type II (\(\beta\)) errors and connect them through power \(=1-\beta\).
Compute the power of a \(z\) test against a specific alternative mean or proportion.
Read and sketch a power curve and the overlapping null/alternative distributions.
Invert a power calculation to find the smallest sample size that reaches a target power.
Identify the three ingredients (\(\sigma\), \(\alpha\), effect size) you must know before planning a study.

title: Chapter 7: Statistical Power
text:
Key ideas

What Power Means
The power of a test is the probability of correctly rejecting \(H_0\) when a particular alternative is true: \(\text{Power}=P(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_0\text{ false})\). High power means the test reliably detects real effects.


Two Kinds of Error
A Type I error rejects a true \(H_0\) (probability \(\alpha\)); a Type II error fails to reject a false \(H_0\) (probability \(\beta\)). Power is exactly \(1-\beta\), so shrinking \(\beta\) raises power.


What Drives Power
Power increases with the effect size, the sample size \(n\), and the significance level \(\alpha\), and decreases with variability \(\sigma\). Since \(n\) and \(\alpha\) are under your control, sample size is the main planning lever.


Computing Power
Translate the rejection rule into a cutoff on the data scale using the null distribution, then assume the alternative is true and find the probability of landing in the rejection region. That area is the power.


Planning the Sample Size
Setting a cutoff under \(H_0\) equal to a cutoff under the desired power gives \(n=\big((z_\alpha+z_\beta)\sigma/(\mu_0-\mu_a)\big)^2\). Smaller effects and lower variability tolerance demand larger samples; always round \(n\) up.

title: Chapter 8: Analysis of Variance
text:
Key ideas

Comparing Several Means
ANOVA extends hypothesis testing to three or more group means at once. The null hypothesis is that all group means are equal; the alternative is that at least one differs.


Partitioning Variation
The total variation \(\text{SSTotal}\) splits into the variation between groups (SSTr, the treatment effect) and the variation within groups (SSE, the error): \(\text{SSTotal}=\text{SSTr}+\text{SSE}\).


The F-Statistic
Dividing each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom gives mean squares, and \(F=\text{MSTr}/\text{MSE}\) compares between-group to within-group variation. A large \(F\) is evidence against equal means.


Multiple Comparisons
A significant \(F\) says the means are not all equal, but not which ones. Pairwise methods such as Fisher’s LSD (higher power) and the Bonferroni adjustment (controls the experiment-wise error rate) locate the differences.

Example: Correlation Does Not Imply Causation

Problem situation: A published study compared sunscreen sales per capita with melanoma (skin cancer) incidence across 24 Northern European countries. Countries that bought more sunscreen had more skin cancer, not less.












The tempting (wrong) conclusion “Sunscreen causes melanoma, so people should stop using it.”


The lurking variable National income. Wealthier countries buy more sunscreen, take more sunny holidays, and detect and report more cancers. In the authors’ multivariate model income stayed significant, but the sunscreen effect did not.


Course reminder \(r\) measures linear association only, and a large \(r\) is equally consistent with reverse causation or a confounding variable.

title: STA258
section: Example: Vehicle Weight and Fuel Economy
text:
Example: Vehicle Weight and Fuel Economy




Problem
The mtcars dataset contains real road-test data for 11 four-cylinder cars.

\(x=\) vehicle weight in thousands of pounds
\(y=\) fuel economy in miles per gallon

Data:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x:&\ 1.513,\;1.615,\;1.835,\;1.935,\;2.140,\;2.200,\\
  &\ 2.320,\;2.465,\;2.780,\;3.150,\;3.190\\[2pt]
y:&\ 30.4,\;30.4,\;33.9,\;27.3,\;26.0,\;32.4,\\
  &\ 22.8,\;21.5,\;21.4,\;22.8,\;24.4
\end{aligned}
\]
Test whether the slope differs from 0.


Hypotheses
\[
H_0:\beta_1=0,
\qquad
H_A:\beta_1\ne0
\]
The reference distribution is \(t_9\).


Conclusion
Since the p-value is about 0.014, reject \(H_0\) at the 5% level.
There is evidence of a negative linear relationship between vehicle weight and fuel economy for these four-cylinder cars.



Calculation
From least squares:
\(\hat y=39.571-5.647x\), \(SSE=99.937\), \(S_{xx}=3.244\), \(n=11\).

1. Estimate the error variance
\(s^2=\dfrac{SSE}{n-2}=\dfrac{99.937}{11-2}
=\dfrac{99.937}{9}=11.104\)
\(s=\sqrt{11.104}=3.332\)

2. Standard error of the slope
\(SE(\hat\beta_1)=\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}
=\dfrac{3.332}{\sqrt{3.244}}
=1.850\)

3. Test statistic
\(t=\dfrac{\hat\beta_1-0}{SE(\hat\beta_1)}
=\dfrac{-5.647}{1.850}
=-3.052\)
\(df=n-2=11-2=9\)

4. Confidence interval for the slope
\(95\%\ CI:\ \hat\beta_1\pm t_{0.975,9}SE(\hat\beta_1)\)
\(=-5.647\pm2.262(1.850)\)
\(=(-9.832,\;-1.462)\)

section: Example: File Size and Download Time
text:
Example: File Size and Download Time




Problem
A controlled network test downloads eight files using the same connection and server.
For each download:

\(x=\) file size in MB
\(y=\) download time in seconds

The fitted line is:
\[
\hat{y}=1.425+0.0992x
\]
Test whether the slope differs from 0.


Hypotheses
\[
H_0:\beta_1=0,
\qquad
H_A:\beta_1\ne0
\]
The reference distribution is \(t_6\).


Conclusion
Since the p-value is less than 0.001, reject \(H_0\) at the 5% level.
There is strong evidence of a positive linear relationship between file size and download time under these test conditions.



Calculation
From least squares:
\[
\hat{y}=1.425+0.0992x,
\qquad
SSE=2.908,
\qquad
S_{xx}=16800,
\qquad
n=8
\]
1. Estimate the error variance
\[
\begin{aligned}
s^2
&=\frac{SSE}{n-2}
=\frac{2.908}{8-2}
=\frac{2.908}{6}
=0.485,\\[-1pt]
s
&=\sqrt{0.485}
=0.696.
\end{aligned}
\]
2. Standard error of the slope
\[
\begin{aligned}
SE(\hat{\beta}_1)
&=\frac{s}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}
=\frac{0.696}{\sqrt{16800}}
=0.00537.
\end{aligned}
\]
3. Test statistic
\[
\begin{aligned}
t
&=\frac{\hat{\beta}_1-0}{SE(\hat{\beta}_1)}
=\frac{0.0992}{0.00537}
=18.462,\\[-1pt]
df
&=n-2
=8-2
=6.
\end{aligned}
\]
4. p-value
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{p-value}
&=2P(T_6\ge18.462)\\[-1pt]
&\approx1.63\times10^{-6}\\[-1pt]
&<0.001.
\end{aligned}
\]

text:
Example: Heating Time and Water Temperature


A lab heats a fixed volume of water on the same hot plate and records its temperature during the first five minutes, before boiling.
The fitted line is:
\[
\hat{y}=19.990+12.257x
\]
where:

\(x=\) heating time in minutes
\(y=\) water temperature in °C

Predict the temperature at:
\[
x=2.5
\]
and compare with predicting at:
\[
x=8.
\]


Calculation
For 2.5 minutes of heating:
\[
\hat{y}
=
19.990476\ldots+12.257143\ldots(2.5)
\approx
50.633
\]
This is interpolation because \(x=2.5\) is inside the observed range.
For 8 minutes of heating:
\[
\hat{y}
=
19.990476\ldots+12.257143\ldots(8)
\approx
118.048
\]
This is extrapolation because \(x=8\) is outside the observed range.


Prediction target
The observed heating times only cover:
\[
0\le x\le5.
\]
Predictions inside this range are safer than predictions far outside it.


The 2.5-minute prediction is within the observed range. The 8-minute prediction gives about 118°C, showing why the fitted linear pattern should not be extended far beyond the data.

text:
Example: Concert Ticket Resale Prices


A student tracks fictional resale ticket prices for a concert as the show gets closer.
The fitted line is:
\[
\hat{y}=453.381-12.714x
\]
where:

\(x=\) days before the concert
\(y=\) resale ticket price in dollars

Predict the resale price for:
\[
x=8
\]
and compare it with predicting at:
\[
x=30.
\]
Observed \(x\) values range from 3 to 13 days before the concert.


Calculation
For 8 days before the concert:
\[
\hat{y}
=
453.380952\ldots-12.714286\ldots(8)
\approx
351.667
\]
This is interpolation because \(x=8\) is inside the observed range.
For 30 days before the concert:
\[
\hat{y}
=
453.380952\ldots-12.714286\ldots(30)
\approx
71.952
\]
This is extrapolation because \(x=30\) is outside the observed range.


Prediction target
The observed data only cover the final stretch before the concert:
\[
3 \le x \le 13.
\]
Predictions inside this range are safer than predictions far outside it.


The 8-day prediction is reasonable if the line fits well. The 30-day prediction should be treated carefully because resale markets can behave very differently far away from show day.
